cards.title: Agent Control Boundary
cards.prompt: What is the cost of moving the control boundary toward the model?
cards.answer: More adaptability comes with another run-time decision that can fail.

cards.title: Agent Control Boundary
cards.prompt: What separates a workflow from an agent at the control boundary?
cards.answer: A workflow follows transitions fixed in code; an agent lets the model choose some transitions at run time.

cards.title: Agent Protocol Layer
cards.prompt: How does A2A differ from MCP?
cards.answer: A2A coordinates tasks and artifacts between agent systems; MCP connects a model application to capabilities.

cards.title: Agent Protocol Layer
cards.prompt: What interoperability boundary does MCP standardize?
cards.answer: Application-to-capability access: discovering and connecting to tools, resources and prompts.

cards.title: Agentic Retrieval Routing
cards.prompt: What makes retrieval agentic rather than a fixed RAG stage?
cards.answer: The model decides whether to retrieve, which source or query to use, and whether another hop is needed.

cards.title: Agentic Retrieval Routing
cards.prompt: When is deterministic retrieval preferable to agentic routing?
cards.answer: When one stable source and one search step reliably serve the task.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: What does a large gradient component mean?
cards.answer: The cost is proportionally more sensitive to that weight — a component of 3.2 against 0.1 means the same wiggle moves the cost 32× as much.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: What does a mini-batch trade away, and what does it buy?
cards.answer: It trades gradient accuracy for step frequency — worse estimates taken far more often. Sanderson’s image is a drunk man stumbling downhill quickly against a careful man taking slow deliberate steps.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: What exactly does backpropagation compute?
cards.answer: Gradients through the network’s composed operations. Backpropagation supplies derivatives; an optimizer such as gradient descent decides how those derivatives update parameters.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: What goes wrong if a step follows the wishes of a single training example?
cards.answer: That example wants only its own label. Followed alone, the incentive is to classify everything as a 2 — the gradient is the average over examples for a reason.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: What is the "backward" in backpropagation actually doing?
cards.answer: Propagating wishes. Activations cannot be set directly, so each output neuron records the nudge it wants from the previous layer; the conflicting wishes are summed and the procedure recurses onto the weights and biases that produced them.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: What is the only thing that changes when layers are wider than one neuron?
cards.answer: The derivative with respect to a previous activation becomes a sum over paths of influence, because that neuron reaches the cost through every neuron in the next layer. The weight derivative is the same three-factor product.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: Which three levers can raise a neuron's activation?
cards.answer: Its bias, its incoming weights, and the activations feeding it. The bias is the simplest because its effect on the weighted sum is constant.

cards.title: Backpropagation
cards.prompt: Why is a weight adjusted in proportion to its incoming activation?
cards.answer: Because that activation is how much the weight actually moves the sum — formally ∂z/∂w = a. A weight attached to a barely-active neuron has little leverage over the output.

cards.title: Bias/Variance Tradeoff
cards.prompt: A model has high training error close to its test error. What is wrong and what fixes it?
cards.answer: High bias — it is underfitting. The remedy is more capacity: complexify the model, add features, train longer. Regularising or adding data would make it worse.

cards.title: Bias/Variance Tradeoff
cards.prompt: What problem is k-fold cross-validation solving?
cards.answer: A single train/test split gives a noisy estimate, dependent on one arbitrary partition. Averaging the error over k folds stops the verdict from resting on where the split happened to fall.

cards.title: Bias/Variance Tradeoff
cards.prompt: What single intuition do Mallow's Cₚ, AIC, BIC and adjusted R² share?
cards.answer: That complexity must pay for itself. Each penalises parameter count, so an added parameter only improves the criterion if it buys more fit than it costs.

cards.title: Bias/Variance Tradeoff
cards.prompt: Which way does k move bias and variance in k-nearest neighbours?
cards.answer: Higher k means higher bias and lower variance — averaging over more neighbours smooths the prediction. One hyperparameter spans the whole tradeoff.

cards.title: Bias/Variance Tradeoff
cards.prompt: Why does LASSO double as variable selection where Ridge does not?
cards.answer: The L1 penalty shrinks coefficients to exactly zero, which drops those variables from the model. Ridge’s squared penalty makes coefficients small but never removes them.

cards.title: Bias/Variance Tradeoff
cards.prompt: Why is a low training error uninformative on its own?
cards.answer: Because the diagnosis lives in the gap. Low training error close to test error is a fitted model; low training error far below test error is overfitting. The same number means opposite things depending on the pair.

cards.title: Classification Error Trade-offs
cards.prompt: Why should precision and recall be reported together?
cards.answer: A threshold can improve one by sacrificing the other. Reporting only one hides the operating point and therefore hides which error was made cheaper.

cards.title: Component-Wise RAG Evaluation
cards.prompt: What is the difference between context precision and context recall?
cards.answer: Precision asks how much retrieved material is relevant; recall asks how much required evidence was recovered.

cards.title: Component-Wise RAG Evaluation
cards.prompt: Why can an end-to-end answer score not diagnose a RAG system?
cards.answer: It cannot tell whether evidence was missed during retrieval or mishandled during generation.

cards.title: Context Engineering
cards.prompt: What did attention do to the long-dependency problem rather than solve?
cards.answer: It moved it. Distance within the window became free, and the window itself became the constraint — so the problem reappears one layer up as how to spend a finite context budget.

cards.title: Context Engineering
cards.prompt: What does an agent status bar give the model that the transcript alone does not?
cards.answer: Where it is in the task. The conversation records what was said; injected meta-information about the trajectory lets the model reason about its own progress through a long run.

cards.title: Context Engineering
cards.prompt: What single problem do compression, retrieval and memory hierarchies all answer?
cards.answer: That more relevant information exists than fits. Each is a different way of choosing what makes it into a finite window.

cards.title: Context Engineering
cards.prompt: Where does the eyes/hands split between context and tools break down?
cards.answer: Tool definitions live in the context. So the observation space contains a description of the action space — what the agent sees includes what it can do.

cards.title: Context Engineering
cards.prompt: Why does prompt ordering affect latency and cost?
cards.answer: The KV cache survives only up to the first change. Putting the stable parts first and the volatile parts last keeps the cached prefix valid across turns — an inference detail that dictates application architecture.

cards.title: Context Engineering
cards.prompt: Why is context the binding constraint before model quality is?
cards.answer: The model cannot act on what was never put in front of it. However capable the policy, its ceiling is set by what the context actually contains.

cards.title: Diffusion Guidance
cards.prompt: How does classifier-free guidance avoid a separate classifier?
cards.answer: One model learns both conditional and unconditional predictions, whose difference steers sampling.

cards.title: Diffusion Guidance
cards.prompt: What does a higher diffusion guidance scale trade away?
cards.answer: Diversity and sometimes artifact-free samples, in exchange for stronger condition adherence.

cards.title: Diffusion Noise Prediction
cards.prompt: What target does the standard simplified diffusion objective predict?
cards.answer: The known noise added to the clean sample.

cards.title: Diffusion Noise Prediction
cards.prompt: Why can diffusion training corrupt a clean sample at any chosen timestep directly?
cards.answer: The forward Gaussian process has a closed form, so earlier corruption steps need not be simulated.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: Every final-layer vector predicts what follows it. What does that buy, and what does it require?
cards.answer: It buys training efficiency — one passage becomes many training examples. It requires masking, because a prediction made at an early position must not see the later tokens that would give away its answer.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: How do you test whether a direction in embedding space means what you think?
cards.answer: Dot it against words you have opinions about. Take cats − cat as a candidate plurality direction and plurals score higher; one through four give increasing values, which is the direction measuring degree rather than just membership.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: What are logits, and what turns them into a prediction?
cards.answer: The raw unnormalised values the unembedding matrix produces, one per vocabulary token. Softmax converts them into a probability distribution.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: What is a token's vector at the moment it leaves the embedding matrix?
cards.answer: A lookup with no input from its surroundings — it encodes that token and nothing else. Everything that follows exists to make that stop being true.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: Why does Sanderson qualify the king − man + woman ≈ queen example?
cards.answer: In the model he used, queen sits farther off than the difference predicts — presumably because queen is not used in training data as merely a feminine king. Family relations demonstrate the property more cleanly.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: Why is enlarging the context window not simply a matter of allocating more memory?
cards.answer: The attention pattern is the square of the context size. Doubling the window quadruples that cost, which is why the limit that made early ChatGPT lose the thread was hard to lift.

cards.title: Embedding
cards.prompt: Why must the last vector in a mystery novel carry the whole plot?
cards.answer: Because it is the only vector used for the prediction. A vector that started life embedding “was” has to have absorbed everything in the context relevant to naming the murderer.

cards.title: Estimation and Uncertainty
cards.prompt: How do estimator bias and sampling variance differ?
cards.answer: Bias is the expected offset from the target; variance is how estimates change across possible datasets.

cards.title: Estimation and Uncertainty
cards.prompt: What does a frequentist confidence interval describe?
cards.answer: Repeated-sampling coverage, not the probability that a fixed parameter lies in one realized interval.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: What do clustering metrics like the silhouette coefficient actually measure?
cards.answer: Whether the clusters are dense and well separated — a property of the partition, not of its correctness. With no ground truth available, the metric answers a question adjacent to the one being asked.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: What does a learned metric inherit that a formula-defined one does not?
cards.answer: A training distribution. It is only valid where it has seen data — and unlike a formula, an optimiser can be pointed at the regions where it is wrong.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: What does the medical-diagnosis example establish about single-number scores?
cards.answer: That a false negative and a false positive are not comparable events. A missed diagnosis and a false alarm cost different things, and any single number has already assumed they cost the same.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: What error does BERTScore stop punishing?
cards.answer: Paraphrase. Scoring by embedding similarity rather than n-gram overlap means a correct answer in different words is no longer counted as wrong.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: What failure does perplexity miss that burstiness catches?
cards.answer: Endless repetition. A model can predict held-out data well while producing no variety at all, so a good perplexity score says nothing about the diversity of what it generates.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: Why is BLEU precision-oriented and ROUGE recall-oriented?
cards.answer: Because of the tasks they were built for. Translation asks whether what was produced is correct — precision. Summarisation asks whether what mattered was kept — recall.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: Why is choosing a metric a modelling decision rather than a reporting one?
cards.answer: Each metric encodes a judgement about which errors matter. Picking one has already decided what the system is allowed to get wrong.

cards.title: Evaluation Metrics
cards.prompt: Why is precision/recall confused with sensitivity/specificity so often?
cards.answer: They are the same confusion matrix read by two communities using different denominators. The cells are identical; only what each figure is divided by differs.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: If exploration is expensive, what is the lever Li says matters most?
cards.answer: The environment and data, over the algorithm. Since every sample costs, the thing you explore in determines the return on exploring more than the rule choosing what to try.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: What does an upper-confidence-bound method prefer, and why is that exploration?
cards.answer: Actions whose value is uncertain, not merely high. Uncertainty is where new information lives, so favouring it buys knowledge rather than immediate return.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: What happens to generated text at near-zero sampling temperature, and why?
cards.answer: It collapses into a literal infinite loop. Always taking the most confident token is pure exploitation, so the model re-enters the same state and repeats — Karpathy’s example loops endlessly about startups.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: What two separate difficulties does a sparse, delayed reward create?
cards.answer: Finding the rewarded sequence at all, which may take very many trials, and then working out which of its actions earned the reward. Discovery and credit assignment are distinct problems.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: Where does the exploration/exploitation trade-off invert, and why?
cards.answer: In RLHF. Because the reward signal is only trustworthy near the training distribution, unconstrained exploration finds the reward model’s mistakes — so the KL penalty deliberately limits exploring rather than encouraging it.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: Where is exploration in the Q-learning update?
cards.answer: Nowhere. The max is exploitation stated in one symbol; nothing in the equation says how the agent finds actions worth maximising over. ε-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling are all bolted on to supply exactly that gap.

cards.title: Exploration vs. Exploitation
cards.prompt: Why does sample inefficiency disqualify RL in robotics or healthcare rather than merely slow it?
cards.answer: Because each interaction has a real cost in money, time or hardware. Methods needing millions of environment interactions are unaffordable in those settings, not just protracted.

cards.title: Gradient Descent
cards.prompt: Newton's method converges in far fewer steps. Why is deep learning first-order anyway?
cards.answer: The Hessian. Forming and inverting a second-derivative matrix over a modern network’s parameter count is unaffordable, and that single cost is why the whole field stays first-order.

cards.title: Gradient Descent
cards.prompt: What distinguishes one model from another, if they all share the same optimiser?
cards.answer: The loss and the hypothesis class. Linear regression, logistic regression and a neural network differ in what they are fitting and what they are penalised for — the update rule is the same for all three.

cards.title: Gradient Descent
cards.prompt: What does gradient descent actually guarantee about the point it reaches?
cards.answer: Only that the gradient vanishes there, within whatever basin it started in. Nothing about global optimality — that it works on non-convex objectives is an empirical fact the field relies on without fully explaining.

cards.title: Gradient Descent
cards.prompt: What is Adam or RMSProp chosen for in practice?
cards.answer: Stability, not speed. Per-parameter adaptive rates keep updates from blowing up, which is the reason Karpathy gives for using them.

cards.title: Harness Engineering
cards.prompt: Once competitors have comparable models, where does the difference between their agents live?
cards.answer: In the harness. The model becomes a commodity component; what is built around it — constraints, verification, recovery — is what still differs.

cards.title: Harness Engineering
cards.prompt: What does MAST's "missing task verification" group correspond to in harness terms?
cards.answer: The Verify layer, absent. An agent that can report “completed” with nothing checking the result against requirements has a hole prompt tuning cannot close.

cards.title: Harness Engineering
cards.prompt: What three terms does the harness add to Agent = LLM + Context + Tools?
cards.answer: Constrain, Verify and Correct — what the agent may do, whether it did it correctly, and how to recover when it did not. The first two terms describe capability; these three describe reliability.

cards.title: Harness Engineering
cards.prompt: Which three failures of the bare ReAct loop does a harness exist to absorb?
cards.answer: Hallucinating tools or parameters that do not exist, picking the wrong tool, and being unable to recover from an error.

cards.title: Harness Engineering
cards.prompt: Which two multi-agent failures does MAST's dialogue-focused taxonomy miss?
cards.answer: Concurrency conflicts when several agents share a file system, and cascading amplification of an error across agents. Both come from engineering practice rather than from conversation traces.

cards.title: Hybrid Retrieval
cards.prompt: What happens after hybrid retrieval pools candidates from several channels?
cards.answer: Scores are normalized or rank-fused before the candidates are reranked.

cards.title: Hybrid Retrieval
cards.prompt: Why combine sparse and dense retrieval?
cards.answer: They fail differently: sparse retrieval preserves exact terms, while dense retrieval catches paraphrases.

cards.title: Long-Term Dependency
cards.prompt: How is RL credit assignment the same problem as long-term dependency?
cards.answer: Both ask which distant thing accounts for something here — an early action for a late reward, an early word for a late prediction. Same structure, and the mitigations rhyme: reward shaping and eligibility traces where sequence models use gating.

cards.title: Long-Term Dependency
cards.prompt: In what sense does attention convert the long-dependency problem rather than solve it?
cards.answer: It turns a depth problem into a width problem. Distance becomes free, and total sequence length becomes the cost — which is why the finite context window is now the binding constraint.

cards.title: Long-Term Dependency
cards.prompt: What does a void function that returns a value diagnose in generated code?
cards.answer: A long-range interaction failure. The local syntax is correct because it depends on nearby tokens; the signature is far enough back that the model no longer holds it. Fluent in form, wrong across distance.

cards.title: Long-Term Dependency
cards.prompt: Why is the RNN long-dependency failure practical rather than theoretical?
cards.answer: RNNs can represent such dependencies — a human can hand-pick parameters that solve toy versions. What fails is learning them by gradient descent, not representing them.

cards.title: Matrix Calculus for Learning
cards.prompt: How do a gradient and a Hessian differ?
cards.answer: The gradient gives first-order sensitivity; the Hessian describes local curvature through second derivatives.

cards.title: Matrix Calculus for Learning
cards.prompt: Why can a matrix-calculus identity sheet not prove an optimizer is well behaved?
cards.answer: Shape, invertibility and regularity conditions still have to hold.

cards.title: Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning
cards.prompt: Why can one-shot retrieval fail on a multi-hop question?
cards.answer: The original query may not resemble passages whose identity is only revealed by an earlier result.

cards.title: Multi-Hop Retrieval Planning
cards.prompt: Why must a multi-hop system retain provenance at every hop?
cards.answer: An early wrong entity can redirect every later search while leaving a fluent final answer.

cards.title: Offline Policy Evaluation
cards.prompt: What makes offline policy evaluation fundamentally counterfactual?
cards.answer: The target policy may choose actions that the behaviour-policy log rarely or never contains.

cards.title: Offline Policy Evaluation
cards.prompt: What tradeoff separates direct methods from importance sampling in OPE?
cards.answer: Direct models introduce model bias; importance weights can introduce very high variance.

cards.title: On- vs Off-Policy Learning
cards.prompt: What determines whether learning is on-policy or off-policy?
cards.answer: Whether the data-generating behaviour policy is the same policy being learned about.

cards.title: On- vs Off-Policy Learning
cards.prompt: What does off-policy learning gain and risk?
cards.answer: It gains data reuse and sample efficiency but risks distribution mismatch and unstable correction.

cards.title: RAG vs Long Context
cards.prompt: How do long context and RAG allocate evidence differently?
cards.answer: Long context sends more of the corpus; RAG searches first and sends a selected subset.

cards.title: RAG vs Long Context
cards.prompt: What is the characteristic evidence failure of each approach?
cards.answer: Long context may ignore available evidence; RAG may exclude the needed evidence before generation.

cards.title: Rank-Aware Evaluation
cards.prompt: What does normalisation add after DCG has already included rank position?
cards.answer: It compares the observed ordering with the best ordering available for that list, allowing scores from lists with different attainable gains to be averaged.

cards.title: Reference-Based Text Evaluation
cards.prompt: What limitation do BERTScore and MoverScore address that BLEU and ROUGE retain?
cards.answer: They allow semantically similar paraphrases to match even when surface n-grams differ. They change the definition of similarity rather than eliminating dependence on a reference.

cards.title: Reflection-Evaluator Loop
cards.prompt: What are the four stages of a reflection-evaluator loop?
cards.answer: Draft, evaluate, turn findings into feedback, then revise.

cards.title: Reflection-Evaluator Loop
cards.prompt: Why are external checks valuable in a reflection loop?
cards.answer: A model critiquing itself can repeat the same blind spots as its draft.

cards.title: Regression Loss Geometry
cards.prompt: Why can MAE and RMSE rank the same models differently?
cards.answer: MAE weights residual magnitude linearly, while RMSE inherits squared-error emphasis on large misses. The disagreement reports a choice about whether tail errors should dominate.

cards.title: Retrieval Chunking Boundary
cards.prompt: What is the central chunk-size tradeoff in retrieval?
cards.answer: Small chunks match precisely but lose context; large chunks preserve context but add noise and cost.

cards.title: Retrieval Chunking Boundary
cards.prompt: Why is there no corpus-independent optimal chunk size?
cards.answer: Document structure, query granularity, task, model limits and synthesis budget all change the useful boundary.

cards.title: Retrieval-Reranking Funnel
cards.prompt: What is the reranker buying with its extra computation?
cards.answer: More precise selection of the small evidence set that deserves prompt space.

cards.title: Retrieval-Reranking Funnel
cards.prompt: Why does a retrieval-reranking funnel use a broad first stage?
cards.answer: The first stage cheaply maximizes recall over a large corpus.

cards.title: Reward Proxy Failure
cards.prompt: Why can a reinforcement-learning agent satisfy its reward while failing the task?
cards.answer: It optimizes the measurable proxy it receives, not the designer’s unobserved intention.

cards.title: Reward Proxy Failure
cards.prompt: Why can reward shaping create new failure modes?
cards.answer: Every added intermediate signal becomes another target the agent can optimize independently of the real objective.

cards.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
cards.prompt: Beyond opportunity cost, how does built-in knowledge actively harm later progress?
cards.answer: It complicates the system in ways that make it worse at exploiting general computation. The structure added to help does not merely stop paying — it obstructs the method that would have scaled.

cards.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
cards.prompt: What distinguishes an architecture that lasts from one that plateaus?
cards.answer: What it encodes. A lasting architecture encodes how to spend compute — parallelism, modality-indifference. A plateauing one encodes what is true about the domain, like phonemes or parse structure.

cards.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
cards.prompt: What false assumption makes knowledge engineering look like the right move?
cards.answer: That available compute is fixed. Under that assumption domain knowledge is the only lever; over a horizon longer than one research project, far more compute arrives anyway, and only methods that can absorb it keep improving.

cards.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
cards.prompt: What should be built in, if not knowledge about the domain?
cards.answer: The meta-methods that find complexity. The contents of minds are irredeemably complex and the world they describe is endless, so the buildable thing is the capacity to discover, not the discoveries.

cards.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
cards.prompt: Which two methods does Sutton say scale arbitrarily, and what do they share?
cards.answer: Search and learning. Both convert compute into performance with no human in the loop, which is why more hardware improves them without more research.

cards.title: Scaling Beats Knowledge Engineering
cards.prompt: Why is the lesson "bitter" rather than merely surprising?
cards.answer: Because the breakthrough arrives by the route the researchers rejected. Every win for scale is a defeat for a favoured human-centric approach, so it is resented and incompletely digested instead of learned once.

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: What are the three roles a query, a key and a value play?
cards.answer: The query is what this position is looking for, the key is what a position offers for matching, and the value is what actually gets carried across once the match is scored. Query·key decides how much of the value to absorb.

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: What does attention make free, and what does it make expensive?
cards.answer: Distance becomes free — position 1 and position 500 are one hop apart. Total length becomes expensive, because every pair of positions is compared: O(n²) where recurrence was O(n).

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: What does the softmax step do to the attention scores?
cards.answer: Makes them positive and sum to 1, so they act as weights over the value vectors — the irrelevant positions are scaled toward zero and drowned out of the sum.

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: What failure mode does a single attention head have?
cards.answer: Its own position’s value tends to dominate the weighted sum, so little context actually gets absorbed. Several heads give several subspaces, letting one bind “it” to “the animal” while another binds it to “tired.”

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: What single change turns self-attention into cross-attention?
cards.answer: Taking the queries from one source and the keys and values from another. That one substitution lets the mechanism fuse two different kinds of data, which is what made one architecture serve text, images and audio.

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: Why divide the attention scores by √d k before the softmax?
cards.answer: For gradient stability. Dot products grow with dimension, and large scores push the softmax into its flat region where gradients vanish.

cards.title: Self-Attention
cards.prompt: Why does pronoun resolution defeat a model that only attends locally?
cards.answer: The antecedent can be arbitrarily far away, and several candidates may sit nearby. Resolving which “it” is which requires connecting every word to every other, not just to its neighbours.

cards.title: Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics
cards.prompt: When does a multi-agent design earn its coordination cost?
cards.answer: When intrinsic decomposition, parallel work or an independent verifier produces measured gains.

cards.title: Single- vs Multi-Agent Economics
cards.prompt: Why is one agent the recommended baseline?
cards.answer: It preserves global context, avoids handoffs and keeps the token budget in one reasoning trajectory.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: How did the explanation for uninterpretable weights change between 2017 and 2024?
cards.answer: From “the network settled into a happy local minimum” to “clean single-feature neurons may not be what a well-trained network wants at all.” The observation is the same; the second reading makes it a property rather than an accident.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: How would superposition explain why scaling works so well?
cards.answer: Because capacity grows exponentially with dimension rather than linearly, a bigger model gets disproportionately more room for ideas — not merely proportionally more. Sanderson offers this as a candidate mechanism, not a result.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: What does relaxing "perpendicular" to "nearly perpendicular" buy?
cards.answer: The capacity stops being n and starts growing exponentially with dimension. Tolerating a little interference between features is what lifts the hard ceiling the definition of dimension seemed to impose.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: Which parameter dominates how many features a space can hold?
cards.answer: The angular tolerance. At 89°–91° the capacity is uninteresting below ~250,000 dimensions; at 85° the same 12,288-dimensional space holds well over 40 billion directions.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: Which part of the "one neuron stores one fact" account survives superposition, and which does not?
cards.answer: The mechanics survive — rows are directions that ask, columns are edits that answer. What does not survive is the assumption that either corresponds to a single human-legible concept.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: Why can't a feature be one neuron, if a layer exploits superposition?
cards.answer: There are more features than neurons. Once a layer probes orders of magnitude more directions than it has units, each feature must be carried by a specific combination of them.

cards.title: Superposition
cards.prompt: Why is superposition counterintuitive to reason about?
cards.answer: Because in low dimensions the near-perpendicular relaxation buys almost nothing. The exponential behaviour only shows up at high dimension, so small-space intuition points the wrong way.

cards.title: Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping
cards.prompt: What does TD gain and risk by updating before a trajectory ends?
cards.answer: It gains earlier, lower-variance updates but inherits bias from an inaccurate successor estimate.

cards.title: Temporal-Difference Bootstrapping
cards.prompt: Why is temporal-difference learning called bootstrapping?
cards.answer: One learned successor-value estimate is used to train the current value estimate.

cards.title: Tool Interface Design
cards.prompt: What four things must a usable tool contract make legible?
cards.answer: Selection, invocation, outcome and recoverable failure.

cards.title: Tool Interface Design
cards.prompt: Why is a schema insufficient to make a tool call correct?
cards.answer: It constrains argument syntax, not whether the action is intended, authorized or appropriate.

cards.title: Value, Return, and Advantage
cards.prompt: How does return differ from value in reinforcement learning?
cards.answer: Return is realized on one trajectory; value is an expectation over possible returns under a policy.

cards.title: Value, Return, and Advantage
cards.prompt: What does advantage measure?
cards.answer: How much better or worse an action is than the policy’s average action in that state.

cards.title: Diffusion Models
cards.prompt: How does a diffusion latent differ from a VAE latent?
cards.answer: It has the same dimensionality as the data, and the procedure that produces it is fixed rather than learned. Nothing about the encoder is trained — the model’s entire job is denoising.

cards.title: Diffusion Models
cards.prompt: The true reverse conditional is intractable. What makes the training objective computable anyway?
cards.answer: Conditioning additionally on x0. The reverse posterior is then Gaussian, so the variational bound reduces to KL divergences between Gaussians, which have closed forms.

cards.title: Diffusion Models
cards.prompt: What does classifier-free guidance remove from the classifier-guidance recipe?
cards.answer: The separately trained classifier. Conditional and unconditional models are trained jointly and interpolated at sampling time, so steering needs no second network — which is what text-to-image systems actually run on.

cards.title: Diffusion Models
cards.prompt: What makes diffusion training feasible despite the chain having many steps?
cards.answer: xt can be sampled directly from x0 in closed form. Training jumps to a random timestep and denoises there, so it never has to simulate the chain step by step.

cards.title: Diffusion Models
cards.prompt: What price does diffusion pay for tractability, and why was it the affordable one?
cards.answer: Slow sampling — many reverse steps per sample. It was affordable because inference cost yields to distillation and latent-space training, whereas a GAN’s adversarial instability cannot be engineered away as cleanly.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: How does Reflexion detect hallucination operationally?
cards.answer: As a run of identical actions producing identical observations. The agent is repeating itself and learning nothing, which is a signal available without knowing what the right answer was. Chain of Hindsight conditions on a sequence of past outputs annotated with feedback and ranked by reward.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: What did MRKL's arithmetic failure show about tool use?
cards.answer: That the hard part is knowing when and how to call a tool, not the tool itself. Their 7B model could not reliably extract the arguments from a verbal problem even though the calculator it needed was available and perfectly reliable.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: What distinguishes an agent's short-term memory from its long-term memory?
cards.answer: Short-term is in-context learning, bounded by the context window. Long-term is an external vector store queried at retrieval time — which is retrieval-augmented generation under another name.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: What does long-horizon planning break on?
cards.answer: Revising a plan after an unexpected error. Trial and error is where humans learn most, and it is the case LLM planners handle worst.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: What is the reinforcement-learning reading of Agent = LLM + Context + Tools?
cards.answer: LLM ↔ policy, Context ↔ observation space, Tools ↔ action space. It makes an LLM agent an RL agent whose policy happens to be a language model, rather than a slogan.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: What made MAST conclude multi-agent failures are design flaws rather than bugs?
cards.answer: Simple fixes bought ChatDev only 15.6%. The 14 failure modes cluster into system design, inter-agent alignment and missing verification — categories patching does not reach.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: What separates a workflow from an agent?
cards.answer: Who chose the control flow. In a workflow a human wrote the code paths the model and tools move through; in an agent the model directs its own process and sequences the work.

cards.title: LLM Agent
cards.prompt: Why doesn't a vector store simply solve the finite-context limit?
cards.answer: Its representational power is weaker than full attention. Retrieval extends reach but does not give the model the same access to the retrieved material that having it in context would.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: What default does the cell state invert, relative to a vanilla RNN?
cards.answer: In a plain RNN information decays unless actively preserved; along the cell state it persists unless actively forgotten. Remembering becomes the default rather than the thing the network has to learn.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: What distinguishes the output gate's job from the forget and input gates'?
cards.answer: Forget and input edit the cell state itself; the output gate decides only how much of that state is exposed as this step’s output. The network can hold something it is not currently using.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: What do the LSTM variant comparisons establish?
cards.answer: That no particular gate arrangement matters much — the popular variants perform about the same across large comparisons and searches. The work is being done by the cell-state-plus-gating idea itself.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: What ended the LSTM's dominance, and what did not?
cards.answer: A central factor was parallelism: recurrent step t precedes t+1, while transformer training can process positions in parallel. Accuracy, scaling, and task fit also contributed, and LSTMs were not eliminated.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: What is the significance of a single cell that switches on inside a URL?
cards.answer: The structure was never specified — the model was trained on raw characters. It shows that interpretable, discrete features emerge from character prediction alone, in roughly 5% of cells.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: Why does the cell state only take linear interactions?
cards.answer: Because repeated non-linear transformation is what destroys information across many steps. Keeping the belt to minor linear operations is what lets a signal travel the length of the chain intact.

cards.title: LSTM
cards.prompt: Why is a gate a sigmoid followed by a pointwise multiply?
cards.answer: The sigmoid emits a value in [0, 1] per component, and multiplying by it scales that component between “let nothing through” and “let everything through” — so the gate is a learned, per-component, continuous filter rather than a switch.

cards.title: Markov Decision Process
cards.prompt: What does a policy specify in a Markov decision process?
cards.answer: An action distribution for each state.

cards.title: Markov Decision Process
cards.prompt: What objective does an MDP policy optimize?
cards.answer: Expected discounted return.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: What does an MLP fail to exploit about image data?
cards.answer: That pixels are adjacent. Nothing in the architecture knows about spatial locality, and a pattern learned in one region cannot transfer to another — which is the gap convolution was invented to fill.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: What does the bias contribute that the weights cannot?
cards.answer: A threshold. Weights say which pattern the neuron responds to; the bias says how strong that match has to be before the neuron becomes meaningfully active.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: What happens to a deep network with the non-linearities removed?
cards.answer: Every layer becomes matrix-multiply-plus-offset, so the whole stack collapses into a single linear function. Depth buys nothing without it.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: What is the division of labour between attention and the MLP block?
cards.answer: Attention moves information between positions; the MLP processes each position independently and adds its result back. One supplies context, the other supplies the stored capacity.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: Why are the two MLP matrices read in different orientations?
cards.answer: The up-projection’s rows are directions the input is dot-producted against — each row asks a question. The down-projection’s columns are directions in embedding space — each column is the edit added when its neuron fires. Rows ask, columns answer.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: Why did ReLU displace sigmoid, and why did depth make that decisive?
cards.answer: Sigmoid’s derivative becomes small at both extremes. ReLU keeps a nonzero derivative on its positive side, which often preserves stronger gradients through deep stacks—but it is flat on the negative side and can create dead units.

cards.title: Multilayer Perceptron
cards.prompt: Why do the weights of an edge-detecting neuron carry negatives above and below the band?
cards.answer: A band of positive weights alone sums brightness in a region, which also fires on a solid blob. The negative weights either side make the neuron fire only when the bright region is narrow — an edge.

cards.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
cards.prompt: What changes when RAG becomes agentic?
cards.answer: Retrieval stops being a fixed pipeline stage and becomes a decision the model takes — which store to hit, how many hops, whether to retrieve at all.

cards.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
cards.prompt: What is the argument for keeping facts out of the weights?
cards.answer: Weights are an expensive and uncorrectable place to store a fact; a database is cheap and correctable. Knowledge held outside the model can be audited, updated and cited.

cards.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
cards.prompt: What is the trade between a vector store and a graph store as retrievers?
cards.answer: Dense retrieval is flexible enough to recover paraphrases but can return irrelevant neighbours. Graph retrieval exploits explicit relations, but only relations the system represented and queried correctly. The trade is learned semantic similarity against structured relational coverage.

cards.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
cards.prompt: Which stage of a RAG pipeline carries most of the engineering difficulty?
cards.answer: Retrieval — and re-ranking in particular, the stage most implementations skip. The LLM is the last and least interesting step.

cards.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
cards.prompt: Why can't one aggregate score diagnose a RAG system?
cards.answer: A bad answer can come from perfect retrieval badly used, or from garbage retrieval faithfully used. The two look identical end-to-end and need opposite fixes.

cards.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
cards.prompt: Why doesn't a longer context window simply retire retrieval?
cards.answer: It changes what needs retrieving and moves the cost around rather than removing it. The question is treated as open, not settled by window size.

cards.title: Reward Model
cards.prompt: How does a reward model relate to classical reward design?
cards.answer: It is the same problem past the point where hand-specification is possible. Classical RL shapes a reward function you can write; when you cannot write one at all, you fit one from data instead.

cards.title: Reward Model
cards.prompt: What is a reward model actually approximating, if not a fact?
cards.answer: A disagreement. Human preferences are diverse and do not reduce to one function, so fitting a single scorer to them averages people who genuinely want different answers.

cards.title: Reward Model
cards.prompt: Where do a reward model's absolute scores come from, if it is never shown one?
cards.answer: They are a side effect of consistently ordering pairs. The loss only ever pushes a winner above a loser; a usable scale falls out of doing that consistently across the data.

cards.title: Reward Model
cards.prompt: Why does a reward model have to be learned rather than written?
cards.answer: Nobody can specify “a good answer” as a function, but people can recognise one. Fitting a scorer to recognition is the only route from the judgement that exists to the scalar the optimiser needs.

cards.title: Reward Model
cards.prompt: Why initialise the reward model from the SFT model rather than from scratch?
cards.answer: A scorer has to be at least as capable as the thing it scores. Starting from the policy’s own weights gives it the understanding of the responses it is being asked to rank.

cards.title: Reward Model
cards.prompt: Why is a policy searching for high reward guaranteed to find a reward model's errors?
cards.answer: Because the errors are high scores. Off-distribution mistakes look exactly like the objective, so an optimiser hunting maxima is hunting them specifically — the KL penalty exists to keep it where the scorer is valid.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: By what mechanism would behaviour cloning cause hallucination?
cards.answer: The model imitates answers a human wrote using knowledge the human had and it does not. What it learns from those examples is the habit of producing confident text past the edge of what it knows.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: What breaks if the KL penalty is removed from PPO?
cards.answer: The policy drifts into regions the reward model never saw, where it scores things extremely highly by mistake, and optimisation chases those errors instead of the preference they were meant to stand in for.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: What can demonstration data never tell a model?
cards.answer: How good a response is. Demonstrations show which responses are plausible, so SFT can fix the shape of an answer but cannot rank two answers that are both in the right shape.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: What does ~73% inter-labeler agreement bound?
cards.answer: The reward model’s achievable accuracy. Its training signal is only as consistent as the humans producing it, so roughly a quarter of the comparisons it learns from disagree with each other.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: Why are SFT and RLHF described as unlocking capability rather than adding it?
cards.answer: Pretraining takes ~98% of the compute and all the trillions of tokens. The later phases run on thousands of examples — far too little to install knowledge, but enough to reach knowledge prompting cannot.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: Why does the agent setting reopen credit assignment for RLHF?
cards.answer: RLHF as described scores one response. An agent’s reward arrives only after a long trajectory of tool calls, so something must decide which of those steps earned it.

cards.title: RLHF
cards.prompt: Why does the reward model train on comparisons rather than scores?
cards.answer: Labelers cannot give consistent absolute scores but can reliably say which of two responses is better. The loss only pushes the winner above the loser, and absolute scores emerge from those relative judgements.

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: How does the Transformer escape the Bitter Lesson's verdict on human architectural design?
cards.answer: It encodes almost no knowledge about language. What Sutton says plateaus is built-in domain knowledge; a general method for turning compute into performance is the category he says survives.

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: What does decoder masking do, and why is it necessary?
cards.answer: It sets future positions to −inf before the softmax. Without it, attention over the whole sequence would let a position see the tokens it is supposed to be predicting, so generation would not be causal.

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: What does multi-head attention buy over a single attention head?
cards.answer: Several independently initialised Q/K/V sets give several representation subspaces, so different heads can bind the same word to different antecedents — one head tying “it” to “the animal” while another ties it to “tired.”

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: What does the Transformer pay for removing the recurrence?
cards.answer: Cost quadratic in sequence length (O(n²·d)) instead of linear. Distance between two positions becomes free, but total length becomes expensive — which is why long-context research exists.

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: What is the single adaptation that turns a Transformer into a Vision Transformer?
cards.answer: Cutting the image into 16×16 patches so patches can play the role tokens play. The architecture is otherwise nearly identical to the 2017 original — which is the evidence that it is indifferent to modality.

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: Why can a Transformer train in parallel across a sequence when an RNN cannot?
cards.answer: Positions interact only inside the attention layer. Everything else — feed-forward, residuals, layer norm — acts on each position independently, so there is no step-by-step dependency to serialise on.

cards.title: Transformer
cards.prompt: Why does a Transformer need positional encoding at all?
cards.answer: Order was implicit in the recurrence it removed. With every position attending to every other from layer one, nothing in the architecture distinguishes sequence order, so it has to be added back into the embeddings.

cards.title: Active Reading
cards.prompt: What are the three gates in the active-reading protocol?
cards.answer: Before: scan and activate a schema. During: do not advance without a section summary. After: retrieve without looking, then compare and target the gaps.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: What are protest behaviours?
cards.answer: Escalations — calling more, pushing for the conversation, becoming accusatory — that attempt to re-establish a connection by making its absence more costly to maintain. The intensity is a reconnection strategy, not an attack.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: What can heartbreak specifically disprove for an anxiously attached person?
cards.answer: The nervous system’s core prediction. The abandonment it has spent a lifetime preventing actually happens and is survived, which is direct evidence against the belief that made the vigilance necessary.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: What is the bind inside anxious reassurance-seeking?
cards.answer: The need is real and urgent, and asking for it is itself an exposure that could trigger the withdrawal being feared. The only direct route to relief runs through the risk it is trying to avoid.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: Why can a secure partner feel like less love than an inconsistent one?
cards.answer: Because activation is being read as depth of feeling. A reliable partner produces little prediction error and so little activation, and a nervous system trained on uncertain closeness interprets that calm as the absence of love.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: Why does a small tension trigger a response three levels above it?
cards.answer: The reaction is not to the current moment. The amygdala has matched it against every previous occasion that this kind of tension preceded abandonment, and fired at the weight of the whole set.

cards.title: Anxious Attachment
cards.prompt: Why is anxious hypervigilance a rational strategy rather than a distortion?
cards.answer: The threat-detection system is pattern-matching accurately against its own history. In that history, those small signals genuinely did precede withdrawal — the system is doing exactly the job it was trained for.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: In the pursue-withdraw conflict pattern, what do the two roles have in common?
cards.answer: Both are frightened. The escalation and the withdrawal are two different fear-management strategies learned in two different childhood environments, not a difference in how much either person cares.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: What does it indicate when someone hears criticism of an action as a verdict on their worth?
cards.answer: A history of conditional love, where what you did was who you were. The behaviour and the person were never separated, so a comment on one still lands as a judgement on the other.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: What internal model does secure attachment install?
cards.answer: That others are basically trustworthy and the self is basically worthy of care. Nothing has to be performed to earn love and nothing has to be braced against, which is what produces the ease others find confusing.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: What is the "impossible bind" behind disorganized attachment?
cards.answer: The caregiver was both the source of comfort and the source of fear. The attachment system drives toward them for safety while the threat system drives away, and no coherent strategy can satisfy both.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: Why can a self-aware adult still collapse into a childhood pattern under pressure?
cards.answer: Timing. The limbic attachment circuitry fires faster than the prefrontal cortex, so under real emotional stakes the response is already running by the time the deliberate mind gets to evaluate it.

cards.title: Attachment Theory
cards.prompt: Why does inconsistent caregiving produce a different pattern than consistently cold caregiving?
cards.answer: Consistent unavailability teaches the child to stop expecting a response at all. Inconsistency teaches that the attachment is winnable but unpredictable, so the child develops continuous monitoring instead of shutdown.

cards.title: Attention–Retention Gap
cards.prompt: What does the attention–retention gap measure that screen time alone misses?
cards.answer: Whether spent attention left anything retrievable, actionable, deliberately restorative, or chosen. Equal minutes can produce very different retained value.

cards.title: Audience Fragmentation
cards.prompt: Why is audience fragmentation more costly than ordinary role variation?
cards.answer: Each audience supplies a quantified optimisation target that must be monitored and adjusted. The issue is not having roles; it is letting several external scoreboards compete to define the underlying preference.

cards.title: Avoidance–Relief Loop
cards.prompt: What reward keeps avoidance repeating?
cards.answer: Immediate relief. When withdrawal makes arousal stop, the system learns that escape produced safety and approaches the next similar cue with still less evidence of its own capacity.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: What are deactivating strategies, and when do they fire?
cards.answer: Withdrawal, suddenly noticing the partner’s flaws, idealising singlehood, picking distance-creating fights — and they fire precisely as intimacy deepens, because that is when the nervous system registers threat.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: What lesson installs avoidant attachment?
cards.answer: That needing someone leads to pain. The nervous system’s solution is to stop needing — suppress the vulnerability, build a self-sufficient internal world, and hold people at a functional distance.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: What separates the dismissive avoidant from the fearful avoidant?
cards.answer: The dismissive holds a high self-view and low other-view and genuinely deactivates the need — rarely in conscious distress. The fearful wants connection intensely and fears it simultaneously, oscillating between both patterns.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: Why does pushing an avoidant for closeness make the distance worse?
cards.answer: Pressure is read as threat, and threat is what triggered the deactivation in the first place. What calms the system is predictable low-pressure presence — safety without urgency.

cards.title: Avoidant Attachment
cards.prompt: Why is avoidant self-sufficiency expensive rather than easy?
cards.answer: Because the relationship cannot be used as a regulation resource. Where secure attachment turns toward the partner under stress, the avoidant must self-regulate alone — which looks like coldness and is actually a high-maintenance internal process.

cards.title: Body Composition
cards.prompt: What do the two halves of body composition each signal?
cards.answer: Low body fat reports metabolic health and physical capability; adequate muscle mass reports testosterone-driven fitness. They are separate readouts, which is why either alone is incomplete.

cards.title: Breathing Protocols
cards.prompt: How do activation breathing protocols invert the calming ones?
cards.answer: They hyperventilate rather than extend the exhale — alkalising the blood, dropping CO2 and raising sympathetic activation and adrenaline. The same lever, driven the other direction.

cards.title: Breathing Protocols
cards.prompt: What does high vagal tone actually predict?
cards.answer: How fast you return to baseline after stress. It shows up as better heart rate variability, lower baseline anxiety and better emotional regulation — and breathing practice raises it over weeks.

cards.title: Breathing Protocols
cards.prompt: What makes the 5-5 resonance pattern the one used for building baseline vagal tone?
cards.answer: At roughly 0.1 Hz it synchronises breathing with heart rate variability, which raises basal vagal tone through practice rather than producing a one-off calming effect.

cards.title: Breathing Protocols
cards.prompt: Why does a longer exhale calm you, mechanically?
cards.answer: Inhalation nudges the sympathetic system and briefly raises heart rate; exhalation drives the parasympathetic system through the vagus nerve and lowers it. The longer the exhale relative to the inhale, the stronger the parasympathetic activation.

cards.title: Breathing Protocols
cards.prompt: Why does the physiological sigh need a double inhale?
cards.answer: The second sniff re-inflates alveoli that partially collapsed during stress breathing. That maximises CO2 offloading on the following exhale, and the rapid CO2 drop is what produces the parasympathetic shift.

cards.title: Byproduct Signaling
cards.prompt: What changes when a trait moves from a byproduct signal to a goal signal?
cards.answer: The observer’s account of what the trait points to changes. The trait itself does not reveal whether the account, the motive, or the claimed capability is true.

cards.title: Calibrated Self-Interest
cards.prompt: What calibrates healthy self-interest?
cards.answer: Empathy and reciprocity. Self-respect, pride, and ambition remain healthy when they do not require another person to be diminished, exploited, or made responsible for stabilizing one’s worth.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: How can two people both love genuinely and consistently miss each other?
cards.answer: Because each loves the way they were loved, or the way they wished they had been. Two histories produce two grammars, and neither is failing to give — they are giving in a form the other was not taught to receive.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: What does parentification produce in adulthood?
cards.answer: Inverted boundaries that never righted — compulsive caretaking, an inability to receive care without guilt, and relationships in which the person is permanently the helper.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: Why does the birth-to-seven window carry disproportionate weight?
cards.answer: Plasticity is unusually high, theta activity dominates, and critical filtering is minimal. The environment is absorbed without the capacity to evaluate or reject it, and the encodings are body-level rather than intellectual.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: Why is awareness necessary but not sufficient here?
cards.answer: The patterns are encoded in the nervous system rather than the intellect. Naming one removes its automatic quality, but changing it needs somatic awareness and corrective relational experience, not insight alone.

cards.title: Childhood Wounds and Adult Patterns
cards.prompt: Why is the inheritance framing offered as mechanism rather than blame?
cards.answer: Because most parents are transmitting what they themselves received, without having examined its origin. The wound is generational, so locating it is a description of the transfer rather than an accusation.

cards.title: Circadian Rhythm
cards.prompt: By what mechanism does the body drop its core temperature for sleep?
cards.answer: Peripheral vasodilation — blood is drawn toward the skin, carrying heat away from the core organs. The 1–2°C fall that initiates sleep is achieved by radiating heat outward, not by producing less.

cards.title: Circadian Rhythm
cards.prompt: How does circadian misalignment produce insulin resistance independently of diet?
cards.answer: It decouples the timing of insulin secretion from the timing of glucose intake. The same food arrives when the body is not hormonally prepared to handle it.

cards.title: Circadian Rhythm
cards.prompt: How does morning light determine when you become sleepy 14 hours later?
cards.answer: The morning signal starts the SCN’s countdown to melatonin release, typically 12–16 hours out. The evening sleepiness was scheduled that morning, which is why skipping the light delays it.

cards.title: Circadian Rhythm
cards.prompt: What is a zeitgeber, and which is the strongest one humans have?
cards.answer: A “time-giver” — an external signal that entrains a biological clock. Light is by far the most powerful one the human circadian system responds to.

cards.title: Circadian Rhythm
cards.prompt: What is social jetlag?
cards.answer: The misalignment produced by shifting sleep timing at weekends. The internal clock is pushed later without any travel, which is why Sunday insomnia and Monday grogginess follow the same pattern as crossing time zones.

cards.title: Circadian Rhythm
cards.prompt: Why does circadian misalignment damage every system at once rather than one?
cards.answer: Because the SCN is not a clock you read — it actively synchronises peripheral clocks in the liver, gut, immune system and adrenals. When the master falls out of step, everything it was coordinating desynchronises together.

cards.title: Cognitive Decentering
cards.prompt: What does decentering change without removing resistance?
cards.answer: It stops a momentary thought from automatically defining identity or available behaviour.

cards.title: Cognitive Decentering
cards.prompt: What is the practical sequence of cognitive decentering?
cards.answer: Notice the thought, label it as a mental event, question it, then choose an action.

cards.title: Cold and Heat Therapy
cards.prompt: How does cold-exposure dopamine differ from a cheap dopamine spike?
cards.answer: The source contrasts a longer-lived cold-associated change with rapid repeated rewards. It does not show that every cold exposure improves mood or carries no compensatory cost.

cards.title: Cold and Heat Therapy
cards.prompt: What do heat shock proteins do?
cards.answer: Act as molecular chaperones that repair misfolded proteins — a mechanism implicated in ageing and neurodegeneration, and one proposed pathway for sauna’s association with reduced Alzheimer’s risk.

cards.title: Cold and Heat Therapy
cards.prompt: What is hormesis?
cards.answer: The pattern where something harmful at high dose is beneficial at low dose. The controlled stress provokes an adaptation that leaves the system better off than the exposure cost it.

cards.title: Cold and Heat Therapy
cards.prompt: What transferable skill is trained by staying in the cold?
cards.answer: Staying regulated while the sympathetic system is firing. Choosing to breathe and remain calm inside genuine physiological discomfort is the same capacity every other high-stress situation calls on.

cards.title: Cold and Heat Therapy
cards.prompt: Why cool down between sauna rounds rather than staying in?
cards.answer: The cooling resets the growth hormone signal. Two twenty-minute rounds separated by a cool-down produce the large GH elevation that one continuous session does not.

cards.title: Comfortable Mediocrity Loop
cards.prompt: How can the comfortable mediocrity loop be interrupted without manufacturing a crisis?
cards.answer: Keep the discrepancy visible, remove one easy environmental exit, and convert it into one bounded action. Repetition supplies new identity evidence without requiring danger or deprivation.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: In what sense is perception a "controlled hallucination"?
cards.answer: The brain generates a predictive model of what should be happening and corrects it against sensory input. What is experienced is the model, so reality is inferred rather than seen directly.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: What distinguishes perception from awareness, in this layering?
cards.answer: Awareness is registering input. Perception is the interpretation layer — the brain constructs meaning from partial signals rather than receiving raw data, so it is active reconstruction rather than passive reception.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: What does mapping a neural correlate leave unexplained?
cards.answer: Qualia — the felt quality of the experience. You can specify the full mechanism for seeing red and still not have touched what it is like to see it.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: What does panpsychism claim that physicalism does not?
cards.answer: That consciousness is fundamental to reality rather than emergent from complexity — all matter carries some proto-conscious property, and human consciousness is an elaborate instance of a universal one.

cards.title: Consciousness
cards.prompt: Why is observer distance the functional basis of emotional regulation?
cards.answer: Because nothing can be regulated that has not first been observed. Fused with a thought there is only reaction; the gap between noticing it and acting on it is where any choice exists at all.

cards.title: Constraint Compression
cards.prompt: What is learned when a compressed deadline proves infeasible?
cards.answer: The exercise still identifies essential work, dependencies, and safety or quality constraints. Compression is an inspection tool, not a command to preserve an impossible date.

cards.title: Contextual Interference
cards.prompt: Why can worse performance during practice indicate better learning?
cards.answer: Variable, interleaved conditions remove the previous attempt’s momentum. The learner must select and reconstruct the response, producing errors that feedback can correct and a skill that is less tied to one prepared context.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: What are the four motivations running most of what people say?
cards.answer: The need to impress, to be liked, to dominate, and to be understood. Everyone cycles through all four, but one usually hums underneath nearly everything a given person says.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: What does banter demonstrate that depth alone cannot?
cards.answer: Presence, quickness and security at once — you caught what was said, did something with it, and can be challenged without being threatened. Depth creates intimacy but also weight; banter is the relief.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: What is being felt as "chemistry" between two people?
cards.answer: Neural synchrony. With genuine presence, breathing, micro-expressions and energy align through mirror-neuron mirroring — the sensation is real and the mechanism is neurobiological rather than mystical.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Where does the laugh in genuine humour actually come from?
cards.answer: The accuracy of the observation, not the attempt at wit. Trying to be funny overrides the room; noticing something true and stating it precisely is what lands.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Why are most conversations forgettable even when they go fine?
cards.answer: They are information exchanges, and the brain does not store those. What it retains is emotional state and moments of genuine connection — which covering ground does not produce.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Why can a conversation drain you when nothing obviously went wrong?
cards.answer: A performative exchange costs cognitive effort and returns no reward, which produces a mild cortisol response. The brain is registering a losing trade and starting to look for the exit.

cards.title: Conversation Dynamics
cards.prompt: Why does saying less often produce a better conversation?
cards.answer: Because the memorable part is the other person’s experience of being received. Space to think out loud and feel heard produces “that was a good talk” even when you contributed almost nothing.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: By what mechanism does chronic stress lower sex hormones?
cards.answer: Competition for substrate — cortisol and the sex hormones are built from the same cholesterol-derived steroid precursors, so sustained cortisol production draws down the pathway they share.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: How do starchy carbohydrates at dinner lower evening cortisol?
cards.answer: They supply the thing cortisol exists to mobilize. With blood glucose already available, the HPA feedback loop reads no demand and suppresses further cortisol production.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: What does the "wired and tired" presentation say about the cortisol rhythm?
cards.answer: That it has fully inverted — low in the morning, high in the evening. Late-phase burnout, and the slowest to correct, because the whole rhythm has to be turned back around rather than damped at one end.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: What is cortisol's primary job, underneath its reputation as "the stress hormone"?
cards.answer: Deploying energy — mobilizing glucose into the bloodstream so the brain and body have fuel to wake, focus, or meet a stressor.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: Why does a high morning cortisol peak produce a low evening baseline?
cards.answer: The peak trips the HPA axis’s negative feedback loop — the hypothalamus senses high cortisol and suppresses production for the rest of the day. Without the peak, nothing shuts the system down.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: Why does caffeine on waking produce a harder afternoon crash than caffeine an hour later?
cards.answer: Caffeine extends however much cortisol is already up. Taken before the natural peak completes, it stretches an unfinished peak and steepens the decline behind it; taken after, it extends a finished peak into a smoother curve.

cards.title: Cortisol
cards.prompt: Why does chronic stress specifically damage memory, rather than cognition generally?
cards.answer: The hippocampus carries an unusually high density of glucocorticoid receptors, so sustained cortisol acts on it hardest — mediating structural changes that measurably shrink its volume.

cards.title: Deep Work
cards.prompt: How should an internal open loop be handled during a deep-work session?
cards.answer: Write it down in a trusted place and return to the task instead of solving it mid-session.

cards.title: Deep Work
cards.prompt: What distinguishes deep work from merely spending time at a desk?
cards.answer: One demanding task remains uninterrupted long enough for deeper connections to form.

cards.title: Dopamine Baseline
cards.prompt: If the dopamine from a finished project and from a scroll session are chemically identical, where is the difference?
cards.answer: Entirely downstream, in what each source builds. The brain cannot distinguish them; the lives they produce are what diverge.

cards.title: Dopamine Baseline
cards.prompt: What is receptor downregulation actually doing?
cards.answer: Reducing dopamine receptors in number and sensitivity, as an adaptation to chronic overstimulation. The brain’s own correction for too much signal is to turn down the volume it can hear.

cards.title: Dopamine Baseline
cards.prompt: What is the bootstrapping problem of motivation?
cards.answer: The state needing correction is the one that removes the capacity to correct it. Effortful activity is what rebuilds the reward gradient, and depleted motivation is exactly what makes effortful activity feel impossible.

cards.title: Dopamine Baseline
cards.prompt: What is the difference between tonic and phasic dopamine?
cards.answer: Tonic is the steady background level that serves as the reference point — the baseline. Phasic is the burst fired by a cue, a surprise or a novel stimulus — the spike, measured against that reference.

cards.title: Dopamine Baseline
cards.prompt: Why does a fully predictable life produce almost no dopamine even when nothing is wrong with it?
cards.answer: Dopamine fires on prediction error. A life the brain has completely modelled generates no error, so there is nothing to fire on — the flatness is a signalling fact, not a verdict on the life.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: What distinguishes hard dopamine from easy dopamine, given they are chemically the same?
cards.answer: The effort-to-reward ratio and the delay. Easy dopamine is instant, costless and empty within minutes; hard dopamine is delayed, effortful, and compounds into something that raises the real-world reward gradient.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: What is the realistic timeline for baseline recovery, against the one-day version?
cards.answer: Days 3–7 for withdrawal to stabilise, weeks 2–4 before natural rewards register again, and one to three months for substantial receptor upregulation after heavy use.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: Why deliberately induce boredom before deep work?
cards.answer: To lower the baseline so the work itself becomes the reward source rather than competing with cheaper alternatives. Fifteen minutes of silence turns the session into relief instead of resistance.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: Why does quitting one cheap dopamine source so often produce a new one?
cards.answer: The drive is not switched off by removing a source — it redirects to the nearest available substitute. Quit pornography and the eating goes bad; quit games and the scrolling starts.

cards.title: Dopamine Reset Protocol
cards.prompt: Why is "dopamine detox" a category error?
cards.answer: There is nothing to flush. Dopamine is synthesised continuously and is central to motivation, movement and learning. What the protocol actually changes is the baseline, by letting downregulated receptors recover.

cards.title: Emotional Coherence
cards.prompt: What does emotional coherence protect when evidence threatens a belief?
cards.answer: It protects the identity, belonging, causal story, and meaning organized around the belief; dismissing the evidence can feel cheaper than rebuilding that model.

cards.title: Emotional Literacy
cards.prompt: Why should an emotion be treated as a hypothesis rather than a command?
cards.answer: It contains information about the person’s appraisal and state, but its first explanation may be incomplete or wrong. Naming, contextual checking, and delay preserve the information without surrendering the action to it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: What is "energy" in a social context, stated neurologically?
cards.answer: The aggregate signal of nervous system state — broadcast continuously through micro-expressions, vocal tone, movement quality and breathing rate, and picked up by other nervous systems through co-regulation.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why can't confidence be performed convincingly at close range?
cards.answer: The signals are too fine-grained and too involuntary. Performed confidence has a different acoustic, postural and micro-expression profile from the real thing, and other nervous systems register the mismatch without naming it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why can't presence be summoned mid-conversation by trying harder?
cards.answer: Because the attention was already divided in advance — by the phone in the pocket and the next appointment. Presence is set up before the interaction, not willed during it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why does ordinary undivided attention register as extraordinary?
cards.answer: Because almost nobody gives it. Most people in conversation are planning a reply, monitoring how they look and tracking other commitments at the same time — so full presence is rare enough to be felt as magnetic.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why is presence a prerequisite for reading people rather than a separate skill?
cards.answer: Because the data is subtle and fast — subtext under the words, the shift beneath a topic change, the micro-expression before the controlled response. Half-attention does not have the bandwidth to catch any of it.

cards.title: Energy and Presence
cards.prompt: Why is presence attunement rather than a fixed state?
cards.answer: Because it has to meet the specific person. Matching their energy — animated with excitement, still with seriousness — is what signals that you are actually tracking them rather than performing a constant.

cards.title: Environmental Context Collapse
cards.prompt: Why can one room serving every function make both work and rest harder?
cards.answer: The room has learned incompatible predictions. Entering it no longer supplies a clean cue for either state, so attention must resolve the conflict deliberately.

cards.title: Environmental Design
cards.prompt: What is the central environmental-design move?
cards.answer: Make the desired behavior easy and visible, while making its competitor hard and hidden, so the recurring context rehearses the choice before willpower is needed.

cards.title: Exercise and the Brain
cards.prompt: What is demargination?
cards.answer: The recruitment of white blood cells resting against vessel walls into active circulation, triggered by physical stress such as intense exercise or cold immersion — raising circulating immune cell counts for hours afterwards.

cards.title: Exercise and the Brain
cards.prompt: What is now credited with the runner's high, and why does a run produce insight?
