cards.answer: Anandamide rather than endorphins. It crosses the blood-brain barrier readily and promotes lateral thinking and cross-domain pattern recognition — the same endocannabinoid present in flow.

cards.title: Exercise and the Brain
cards.prompt: What is the evolutionary logic linking aerobic effort to BDNF release?
cards.answer: Sustained exertion signalled either pursuit or escape, and both demanded peak cognition. Physical challenge is therefore read as a cue to upgrade the brain rather than as a drain on it.

cards.title: Exercise and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why does hippocampal neurogenesis matter beyond raw neuron count?
cards.answer: New hippocampal neurons carry pattern separation — telling similar memories apart — and cognitive flexibility. Suppressed neurogenesis costs the nuance, not just the number.

cards.title: Exercise and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why place demanding cognitive work after exercise rather than before?
cards.answer: BDNF, norepinephrine and dopamine stay elevated for two to four hours afterwards. The session is being run on a brain in a measurably higher-performance state.

cards.title: Exercise–Learning Coupling
cards.prompt: What two different jobs does exercise–learning coupling assign to movement and novelty?
cards.answer: Exercise supports the biological supply environment; novel learning recruits and repeatedly uses cells in active circuits. Neither job is identical to the other.

cards.title: Familiarity-Understanding Gap
cards.prompt: What closes the familiarity-understanding gap?
cards.answer: Effortful recall, explanation and application that test whether the idea can actually be used.

cards.title: Familiarity-Understanding Gap
cards.prompt: What creates the familiarity-understanding gap?
cards.answer: Repeated exposure feels fluent, and that fluency is mistaken for retrievable or usable knowledge.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: What does the prisoner's dilemma actually demonstrate?
cards.answer: That individually rational choices can produce a collectively worse outcome. Betrayal is better whatever the other does, so both betray and both land on five years where mutual silence would have cost one.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: What four properties made tit-for-tat win Axelrod's tournament?
cards.answer: It is cooperative, retaliatory, forgiving and transparent — it invites good outcomes, cannot be exploited, escapes mutual-defection loops, and is legible enough that partners learn what to expect.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: What is the arbitrage in recognising a positive-sum game before the other party does?
cards.answer: Terms that look generous under zero-sum logic are merely ordinary under positive-sum logic. The person who sees the frame correctly can offer them and capture disproportionate value.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: Why can a Nash equilibrium be stable and bad at the same time?
cards.answer: Because stability only means no one gains by moving alone. Everyone can be worse off than an alternative arrangement and still be unable to reach it without coordinated movement.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: Why is dominance fast to establish and fragile to hold?
cards.answer: It compels compliance rather than attracting it, which generates resentment and provokes coalitional resistance. It has to be continuously re-imposed, where prestige accumulates goodwill instead.

cards.title: Game Theory (Social Dynamics)
cards.prompt: Why treat almost every interaction as a repeated game?
cards.answer: Because most are, and the asymmetry is stark: the cost of generosity in a genuinely one-shot game is trivial, while an aggressive win becomes expensive the moment the game turns out to be repeated.

cards.title: Health Signaling Theory
cards.prompt: Why can no single feature compensate for poor systemic health, on this theory?
cards.answer: Because the signals are integrated holistically. Symmetry, skin, body composition and secondary sexual characteristics are read together as one inference about genetic quality and vitality, so a deficit shows across the set.

cards.title: Hormone Optimization
cards.prompt: Why is stress management a hormonal intervention rather than a soft one?
cards.answer: Because chronic cortisol lowers testosterone directly. Stress is not adjacent to the endocrine system here — it is one of the suppression pathways acting on it, alongside plastics and processed food.

cards.title: Identity as Behavioral Architecture
cards.prompt: What kind of thing is "I'm not a morning person"?
cards.answer: Not an observation but a neural pattern — one that generates aversion at the alarm, predicts difficulty, supplies justifications, and discounts contrary evidence. Every snooze press reinforces the circuit.

cards.title: Identity as Behavioral Architecture
cards.prompt: What makes pain-identity fusion so difficult to leave?
cards.answer: The statements are true as history and constraining as present identity. The suffering self is the known one, so change requires giving up the only self that has been occupied for something unfamiliar.

cards.title: Identity as Behavioral Architecture
cards.prompt: Why claim an identity before the evidence supports it?
cards.answer: Because a proposed identity can change which options are noticed and made salient. It still has to be converted into behaviour; repetition supplies the evidence that updates the self-model.

cards.title: Identity as Behavioral Architecture
cards.prompt: Why does daily consistency update the identity model faster than occasional intensity?
cards.answer: The model updates on accumulated behavioural evidence, not on dramatic events. Thirty minutes daily casts far more votes than two hours weekly, whatever the total volume.

cards.title: Identity as Behavioral Architecture
cards.prompt: Why does genuine praise fail to land on someone who believes they are incompetent?
cards.answer: The brain resolves the dissonance by dismissing the contradicting experience rather than the identity. The defence runs even against favourable evidence, because consistency is what is being protected.

cards.title: Identity as Behavioral Architecture
cards.prompt: Why does imposing new behaviour on an unchanged identity fail?
cards.answer: The brain generates behaviour consistent with its model of who this person is. Behaviour that contradicts the model registers as error, and the correction arrives as resistance, sabotage or reversion.

cards.title: Limiting Beliefs
cards.prompt: What does tracing a belief's origin accomplish, if it doesn't dissolve it?
cards.answer: It removes the belief’s authority. An offhand remark made to a five-year-old by a stressed parent has no standing as a fact about adult capability, and locating the source is what strips its claim to be one.

cards.title: Limiting Beliefs
cards.prompt: Why do childhood failures encode as identity rather than as data?
cards.answer: Because mature attribution is not yet available. The child cannot register “I haven’t learned this yet” and so encodes the failure directly as “I am not capable of this.”

cards.title: Limiting Beliefs
cards.prompt: Why do limiting beliefs strengthen over time on their own?
cards.answer: Confirmation bias becomes their maintenance system. Confirming evidence is amplified and contrary evidence discarded, so the belief’s evidence base grows while its counter-evidence is systematically thrown away.

cards.title: Limiting Beliefs
cards.prompt: Why doesn't disproving a limiting belief change anything?
cards.answer: Because it is a myelinated pathway, not a proposition. You can know it is wrong while the circuit keeps downregulating approach behaviour and filtering perception — refutation is not the currency it runs on.

cards.title: Limiting Beliefs
cards.prompt: Why is the installation mechanism for limiting beliefs also grounds for optimism?
cards.answer: Because it is symmetrical. The same myelination that laid down the limiting belief installs an empowering one — slower in adulthood without childhood’s theta receptivity, but available and directable.

cards.title: Locus of Control
cards.prompt: How can a person build external locus out of positive events?
cards.answer: By attributing them to luck. If success is credited to circumstance and failure to personal inadequacy, then every outcome — good or bad — becomes evidence that action does not drive results.

cards.title: Locus of Control
cards.prompt: What are the two routes to an external locus of control?
cards.answer: Never having built the causal model — the action-outcome relationship was never experienced — or having had it extinguished, by acting repeatedly without reliable result.

cards.title: Locus of Control
cards.prompt: What does an external locus of control do to effort?
cards.answer: It removes the reason for it. If outcomes are set by luck, other people or circumstance, effort has no predicted effect — so the reduced persistence is a rational consequence of the model, not laziness.

cards.title: Locus of Control
cards.prompt: What makes learned helplessness so damaging beyond the original situation?
cards.answer: The update generalises. Having learned that behaviour does not affect this outcome, the organism stops attempting escape even once escape becomes available — the model outlives the conditions that produced it.

cards.title: Locus of Control
cards.prompt: When is mindset work the wrong intervention for external locus?
cards.answer: When the helplessness is accurate. In an environment where actions genuinely do not affect outcomes, the model is correct — the environmental change is the prerequisite, not the mindset.

cards.title: Locus of Control
cards.prompt: Where does ixcarus locate agency, given that most behaviour is unconscious?
cards.answer: At the system-design level rather than the moment. You cannot reliably override an urge in the instant, but you choose what you practise, what environment you sit in, and what identity you install.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: What makes lucid dreaming neurologically unusual?
cards.answer: It combines two things that normally exclude each other — metacognition, which waking has without immersion, and full dream simulation, which dreaming has without metacognition.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: Why does reality testing use text specifically?
cards.answer: Because text is unstable in dreams — it changes when you look away and back. The waking habit has to run for weeks before it transfers into a dream, where the instability becomes the giveaway.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: Why is rehearsal inside a lucid dream higher fidelity than waking visualisation?
cards.answer: Waking mental imagery fires motor circuits at roughly 30–40% of actual movement; during REM the same imagery fires them at close to 100%.

cards.title: Lucid Dreaming
cards.prompt: Why is Wake-Back-To-Bed the most reliable lucidity technique?
cards.answer: Returning to sleep after five or six hours re-enters REM directly and extends it. Lucid dreams occur almost exclusively in REM, and REM loads the second half of the night.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: How does gaslighting manufacture its own evidence?
cards.answer: The sustained stress it creates raises cortisol, which degrades hippocampal memory reliability. The gaslighter then points at the unreliable memory as proof the target cannot trust their own perception.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What makes an identity lever like "smart people know that…" work without an argument?
cards.answer: It does not assert a claim; it defines what the listener’s self-concept requires. Agreeing is then the only move that keeps them consistent with who they take themselves to be.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does "this closes tomorrow" outperform "sign up now"?
cards.answer: Loss aversion is asymmetric — losing feels worse than an equivalent gain feels good. Framing the offer as a loss to be avoided pulls harder than framing the same offer as a gain to be taken.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does a story slip past the resistance a fact provokes?
cards.answer: A story can recruit simulation and identification, reducing active counter-argument while attention is inside it. That makes narrative persuasive, not immune to later scrutiny.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does alternating warmth and cruelty bind harder than steady warmth?
cards.answer: Unpredictable reward drives more dopamine than consistent reward, and contrast makes the good moments read as better than they are. The resulting pattern is indistinguishable from substance addiction, so leaving is withdrawal.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does offering a small payment make a request less likely to be granted?
cards.answer: It converts a social exchange into a market one. Once the transaction is priced, the small sum is judged against market rates and reads as insulting — where reciprocity had been carrying it.

cards.title: Manipulation Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why leave the moral of a persuasive story unstated?
cards.answer: Because a conclusion the listener draws themselves registers as their own idea, and people commit far harder to ideas they believe they generated than to ones handed to them.

cards.title: Manufactured Division
cards.prompt: What is the bounded form of manufactured division?
cards.answer: A grievance is routed through identity, extreme opponents receive disproportionate attention, and conflict displaces inquiry into shared causes. This can emerge from aligned incentives without proving one hidden controller.

cards.title: Meaning of Life
cards.prompt: What does Camus call "philosophical suicide," and why is it a failure?
cards.answer: Adopting a ready-made belief system to bypass the question rather than answer it. He treats it as intellectually dishonest — the absurd is not resolved, only imported around.

cards.title: Meaning of Life
cards.prompt: What does logotherapy claim is the primary human drive?
cards.answer: Meaning — against Freud’s pleasure and Adler’s power. Frankl’s observation from the camps was that a sufficient why lets a person endure almost any how.

cards.title: Meaning of Life
cards.prompt: What happens to the RAS in the absence of a clear purpose?
cards.answer: It has no filtering instruction. Everything becomes equally relevant or irrelevant, which produces constant decision fatigue and the flatness of experience that drifting is usually described as.

cards.title: Meaning of Life
cards.prompt: What is the absurd hero's form of revolt?
cards.answer: Persisting anyway, in full awareness. He does not pretend the labour carries cosmic significance it lacks — the defiance is in continuing without the delusion, not in escaping the boulder.

cards.title: Meaning of Life
cards.prompt: Why is Sisyphus happy, on this reading?
cards.answer: Because he is fully in the rolling rather than waiting on the summit. Presence with the immediate experience, not arrival, is where the meaning is actually located.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: What do focused attention and open monitoring each train?
cards.answer: Focused attention trains the prefrontal-parietal control network — sustaining and returning attention to one object. Open monitoring trains metacognitive awareness: observing the stream without fixing on any part of it.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: What does quieting the default mode network change outside of meditation itself?
cards.answer: The resting state. The DMN generates mind-wandering, rumination and the constant internal narrative, and practice quiets it during rest as well as during sitting.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: What is meditation actually training, if not relaxation?
cards.answer: Attention. The practice is noticing that attention has moved and returning it — repeatedly, for a set duration. The returning is the exercise, not the stillness.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why are meditation and the attention economy antagonistic rather than complementary?
cards.answer: They condition opposite programs on the same hardware — one trains hyperreactivity to novelty and compulsive checking, the other sustained focus and tolerance for boredom. What decides it is which gets more repetitions.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why does labelling an experience reduce its intensity?
cards.answer: The labelling activates the prefrontal cortex and dampens the amygdala response. Naming an emotion is itself a regulating act, not merely a description of one.

cards.title: Meditation and the Brain
cards.prompt: Why is reduced amygdala reactivity in meditators not emotional suppression?
cards.answer: Because the response is recalibrated rather than blocked. The system is answering to actual threat instead of predicted threat, so the spike is smaller and briefer rather than stifled.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: If melatonin is not a sedative, what does it actually do?
cards.answer: It signals darkness. Its presence lowers core temperature, shifts the autonomic system toward parasympathetic dominance and suppresses cortisol — creating the conditions under which sleep can begin, rather than causing it.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: What are the two biologically distinct melatonins?
cards.answer: Pineal melatonin, secreted into the bloodstream as the body’s darkness signal, and intracellular melatonin, produced inside mitochondria in response to infrared light. The second never enters the blood and acts locally as an antioxidant.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: Why does supplementation have more evidential support in older adults?
cards.answer: Because the deficit is real there. The pineal gland calcifies with age and natural production genuinely declines, where in a younger person late melatonin is usually a behavioural timing problem instead.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: Why is the "teenage night owl" biological rather than behavioural?
cards.answer: Puberty shifts melatonin onset about two hours later. The adolescent is not physiologically ready for sleep at the adult time, which is why school start times before 8:30 AM run against the biology.

cards.title: Melatonin
cards.prompt: Why might a supraphysiological melatonin dose make things worse over time?
cards.answer: It can desensitise melatonin receptors and suppress the body’s own production through negative feedback — so the supplement gradually creates the deficit it was taken to correct.

cards.title: Mental Rehearsal
cards.prompt: What boundary separates mental rehearsal from performance fantasy?
cards.answer: Rehearsal targets a specific real action and feeds into execution and feedback. Fantasy ends at the imagined outcome and therefore cannot correct the model against the environment.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: How does an abundance of options damage satisfaction with any one of them?
cards.answer: It installs a permanently elevated reference point. Knowing hundreds of alternatives exist means every real person is measured against an idealised projection, so the shortfall is architectural rather than about them.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: What happens when the attachment system is activated and then repeatedly frustrated?
cards.answer: It adapts by suppressing the activation. Intimacy cues stop being treated as worth investing in, because the investment has repeatedly gone unreciprocated at the attachment level.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: What have dating apps successfully substituted for the goal users came with?
cards.answer: The process itself. Swiping, matching and the validation become the reward, which keeps people on the app — and the app benefits precisely from the connection not being reached.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: What is limerence for, if it is not love?
cards.answer: It is a recruitment drive — a neurochemical state producing enough obsession to sustain the start of pair-bonding. It has a shelf life of roughly 6–18 months, and what was built underneath it is what remains.

cards.title: Modern Dating Psychology
cards.prompt: Why is eager availability a weak signal in evolutionary terms?
cards.answer: In the ancestral environment it could indicate low status or an absence of other options. Engaged unavailability signals that other demands compete for the person’s time, which reads as status.

cards.title: Money as a Coordination Claim
cards.prompt: What gives a currency token purchasing power on this account?
cards.answer: Social and institutional acceptance in exchange and settlement, not its physical material.

cards.title: Money as a Coordination Claim
cards.prompt: Why does commodity backing not eliminate the coordination problem?
cards.answer: Convertibility still depends on an issuer, reserve rules and a legal settlement system.

cards.title: Motivation-to-Automaticity Bridge
cards.prompt: What role does motivation play in the motivation-to-automaticity bridge?
cards.answer: Temporary scaffolding that starts repetitions during the expensive early phase.

cards.title: Motivation-to-Automaticity Bridge
cards.prompt: Why should intense emotional motivation have an exit condition?
cards.answer: Otherwise continuing requires repeatedly reopening the original wound instead of converting drive into structure.

cards.title: Music as State Regulation
cards.prompt: What makes music a state-regulation tool rather than a magical treatment?
cards.answer: Its combined effects on prediction, motor anticipation, arousal, attention, and learned association can shape what the listener does next; no special tuning frequency is required.

cards.title: Negativity Bias
cards.prompt: Beyond the anxiety from specific content, what does sustained negative media consumption change?
cards.answer: The filter itself. With threat detection turned up, the RAS notices everything potentially bad in the environment and screens out much of what is good, so perceived reality recalibrates.

cards.title: Negativity Bias
cards.prompt: What is the commonly cited exchange rate between negative and positive events?
cards.answer: About five positive events to counterbalance one negative event of equivalent size — which is why a single criticism can outweigh months of praise from the same person.

cards.title: Negativity Bias
cards.prompt: What is the evolutionary logic behind weighting threat above reward?
cards.answer: The costs are asymmetric. A missed food opportunity is recoverable and a missed predator is not, so over-vigilance was cheap and under-vigilance was fatal.

cards.title: Negativity Bias
cards.prompt: Why does gratitude practice have empirical support rather than merely feeling nice?
cards.answer: It is deliberate RAS redirection. Repeatedly attending to the positive builds the pathways that notice it — attention management with a neural mechanism, not naive positivity.

cards.title: Negativity Bias
cards.prompt: Why does maximising engagement automatically mean maximising negative content?
cards.answer: Because attention is disproportionately captured by the negative. Any process optimising for engagement converges on outrage and fear without needing to intend it — ratings data and A/B testing find it independently.

cards.title: Nervous System States
cards.prompt: In nervous-system terms, what makes certain people calming to be around?
cards.answer: Co-regulation. Nervous systems read each other’s micro-expressions, vocal tone and body language, so a ventral-vagal-dominant person emits safety cues that other nervous systems receive and drift toward — no social tactic involved.

cards.title: Nervous System States
cards.prompt: What did the Libet experiments show about the timing of a decision?
cards.answer: The brain shows preparatory activity 200–500 milliseconds before the person consciously reports deciding to act — the conscious report trails the process that produced it.

cards.title: Nervous System States
cards.prompt: What third state does Polyvagal Theory add to the fight-or-flight / rest-and-digest binary?
cards.answer: Dorsal vagal shutdown. When fight or flight is impossible and the threat inescapable, the oldest vagal pathway collapses heart rate, blood pressure and metabolic rate rather than mobilizing — what is usually read as burnout or depression.

cards.title: Nervous System States
cards.prompt: Why can't a miscalibrated threat response be argued out of a person?
cards.answer: Neuroception is subcortical — it assigns the state before conscious perception, so a top-down argument never reaches the mechanism. Recalibration takes accumulated bodily experience of safety instead.

cards.title: Nervous System States
cards.prompt: Why does the sympathetic state become chronic in modern life instead of resolving?
cards.answer: The sequence it evolved for ends in physical action that discharges the mobilized energy. Psychological threats never resolve and nothing is discharged, so the system never gets the signal to return to ventral vagal.

cards.title: Nervous System States
cards.prompt: Why is the breath the fastest lever on nervous system state?
cards.answer: It is the only autonomic function under voluntary control, so it is the one place conscious action reaches the autonomic system directly. Extended exhales raise vagal tone via the Hering-Breuer reflex and baroreceptor signaling.

cards.title: Norm Calibration
cards.prompt: How does a standard differ from a goal in norm calibration?
cards.answer: A goal is a distant outcome; a standard is the floor that current behaviour is expected to meet. Calibration changes when the supporting action becomes ordinary, not when the outcome is merely declared normal.

cards.title: Novelty-Cadence Conditioning
cards.prompt: How is novelty-cadence conditioning retrained?
cards.answer: By gradually extending uninterrupted time with one context before switching.

cards.title: Novelty-Cadence Conditioning
cards.prompt: What response does a rapid novelty feed rehearse when discomfort appears?
cards.answer: Switching immediately to a new stimulus rather than elaborating the current one.

cards.title: Novelty Substitution
cards.prompt: What evidence is missing when novelty is substituted for compatibility?
cards.answer: Behaviour across stress, conflict, routine, care, and repair. Novel intensity reports a state; it does not provide the longitudinal pattern needed to compare relationships.

cards.title: Nutrition and Cognition
cards.prompt: What is the evolutionary logic for fasting raising BDNF?
cards.answer: Scarcity was exactly when cognition mattered most — finding food demanded performance. The brain was built to work well hungry, so the fasted state reads as a cue to sharpen rather than to conserve.

cards.title: Nutrition and Cognition
cards.prompt: What is the metabolic switch during a fast, and when does it arrive?
cards.answer: After roughly 12–18 hours the liver’s glycogen runs down and it begins producing ketones from fat. The brain shifts from glucose to ketone metabolism, which many people register as clarity.

cards.title: Nutrition and Cognition
cards.prompt: Why does gut health show up as mood?
cards.answer: About 90% of serotonin is produced in the gut, and the microbiome also makes precursors for GABA and dopamine metabolites — communicating with the brain via the vagus nerve and immune signalling.

cards.title: Nutrition and Cognition
cards.prompt: Why is diet structural for the brain and not only fuel?
cards.answer: Roughly 60% of the brain is fat, predominantly DHA, and neurotransmitters are built from dietary amino acid precursors. What you eat becomes the substrate, not just the energy running through it.

cards.title: Nutrition and Cognition
cards.prompt: Why must DHA come from the diet?
cards.answer: The brain cannot synthesise enough of it from precursors. It is the primary structural fatty acid of the brain, and low intake tracks with impaired cognition, higher depression risk and reduced neurogenesis.

cards.title: Pattern Over Tells
cards.prompt: What evidence must exist before a behavioral tell supports an inference?
cards.answer: An individual baseline, a deviation, recurrence in comparable contexts, and an audit of plausible alternatives and the observer’s own bias.

cards.title: Pattern Recognition
cards.prompt: What decides whether a pattern match stays automatic or reaches conscious attention?
cards.answer: Routine matches stay automatic; novel or complex cases rise into conscious processing.

cards.title: Pattern Recognition
cards.prompt: Why is a bodily intuition signal not proof that a prediction is correct?
cards.answer: It shows that below-awareness processing produced a conclusion, not that the underlying pattern library was accurate.

cards.title: Perceptual Gating
cards.prompt: What is the difference between perceptual gating and creating reality?
cards.answer: Gating changes which available signals enter the conscious model and how they are interpreted. It does not create external facts; prediction error can still show that the model was wrong.

cards.title: Posture and Movement
cards.prompt: What makes posture the first move among the health signals?
cards.answer: Its cost. Every other signal takes money or time; posture can be corrected immediately at no expense, which puts it ahead of the interventions that need either.

cards.title: Process-Reward Association
cards.prompt: What do stable ritual cues contribute to a process-reward association?
cards.answer: They reduce initiation decisions and make the start of work more predictable.

cards.title: Process-Reward Association
cards.prompt: Why is process-reward association retained as a behavioural claim?
cards.answer: The source invokes dopamine and myelination but supplies no biological measurement.

cards.title: Relationship Medium Substitution
cards.prompt: What is substituted in relationship medium substitution?
cards.answer: An easily observed platform signal substitutes for harder evidence about the relationship. Contact can express care, but its frequency is not identical to intimacy and its absence is not identical to rejection.

cards.title: Response Within Constraint
cards.prompt: How does response within constraint differ from resignation?
cards.answer: It accepts only the part that cannot be changed now, then directs agency toward stance and remaining action. Resignation treats the whole field as fixed.

cards.title: Retaliation Escalation Loop
cards.prompt: What shared assumption does “an eye for an eye” require to produce closure?
cards.answer: Both parties must agree on the original harm, the proportional response and when the balance is settled.

cards.title: Retaliation Escalation Loop
cards.prompt: Why does retaliation tend to escalate when that accounting is disputed?
cards.answer: The recipient experiences payback as a new injury and treats it as justification for another response.

cards.title: Scheduled Commitment
cards.prompt: What decision does a scheduled commitment remove from execution time?
cards.answer: Whether the current mood grants permission to begin. The priority, time, and first action were chosen earlier; execution starts from the cue rather than reopening the goal debate.

cards.title: Seiri (Sort) – Part of the 5S System
cards.prompt: In what sense is decluttering a cognitive intervention rather than an aesthetic one?
cards.answer: The visual cortex processes disorder continuously, drawing on the same resources focus and creativity need. Removing objects buys attention back; the tidiness is a side effect.

cards.title: Seiton (Set in Order) – Part of the 5S System
cards.prompt: Why must seiri precede seiton?
cards.answer: Because arranging what should have been discarded only produces a well-labelled surplus. Sorting decides what exists; setting in order removes the search cost for what survived.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy
cards.prompt: How does early self-efficacy damage become permanent without intervention?
cards.answer: Low efficacy produces avoidance, and avoidance removes any chance of the mastery experience that would revise it. The belief protects itself by preventing the attempt that could disconfirm it.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy
cards.prompt: How does self-efficacy differ from self-esteem?
cards.answer: Self-esteem is a global judgement of worth. Self-efficacy is a specific judgement about capability in a specific domain — high for coding and low for public speaking in the same person, without contradiction.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy
cards.prompt: What separates high and low self-efficacy in how a setback is read?
cards.answer: The attribution. High efficacy attributes the setback to effort or strategy, which can be changed; low efficacy attributes it to ability, which feels fixed — and that reading decides whether there is a next attempt.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy
cards.prompt: Which of Bandura's four sources is the most powerful, and why?
cards.answer: Mastery experience. Actually succeeding builds efficacy for that domain directly, and the loop runs both ways — success invites attempts, failure invites avoidance, which removes the practice that would have produced success.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy
cards.prompt: Why can watching an expert reduce rather than raise your self-efficacy?
cards.answer: Vicarious learning depends on perceived similarity. An expert performing effortlessly reads as a different kind of person; someone who was recently where you are reads as evidence about you.

cards.title: Self-Efficacy
cards.prompt: Why should capability judgements not be made while exhausted?
cards.answer: Physiological and emotional state is one of the four inputs to the efficacy assessment. Fatigue and anxiety get read as evidence of incapability, so a depleted person systematically underestimates themselves.

cards.title: Self-Respect Through Kept Promises
cards.prompt: Why does action come before the feeling in this model of self-respect?
cards.answer: Self-trust is inferred from evidence. Repeatedly keeping a bounded promise supplies evidence that one’s commitments matter; waiting to feel worthy withholds the behavior that could produce it.

cards.title: Shu‑Ha‑Ri (Three Stages of Mastery)
cards.prompt: Why can't you skip Shu and start at Ha?
cards.answer: Because breaking a form you never learned is not innovation but ignorance of what is being broken. Rigid imitation is a phase to pass through, not a failure of originality.

cards.title: Skill Acquisition
cards.prompt: What does practice without decision pressure leave out?
cards.answer: The reading. Real situations require assessing which version of the move fits and what to do when it fails; rehearsing a predetermined sequence encodes the execution without the judgement that selects it.

cards.title: Skill Acquisition
cards.prompt: What is the difference between familiarity and skill?
cards.answer: Familiarity is the ability to perform under the exact conditions you practised in. The brain optimises for the conditions it is given, so stable practice produces performance that collapses the moment anything changes.

cards.title: Skill Acquisition
cards.prompt: What migrates from the prefrontal cortex to the procedural system, and why does the quality of practice matter to it?
cards.answer: Whatever was actually built. Repetition automates the skill either way — comfortable blocked practice migrates a narrow, brittle habit; variable, pressured practice migrates a transferable capability.

cards.title: Skill Acquisition
cards.prompt: Where are knowledge and skill stored differently, and why does it matter under pressure?
cards.answer: Knowledge sits in declarative memory — conscious, slow and metabolically expensive to apply. Skill is encoded procedurally in the basal ganglia and cerebellum, which is why it survives pressure and distraction.

cards.title: Skill Acquisition
cards.prompt: Why does a practice session without mistakes produce no growth?
cards.answer: Learning systems update only on prediction error. With no gap between the expected and the actual, there is nothing to update against — the session maintains the skill rather than building it.

cards.title: Skill Acquisition
cards.prompt: Why does interleaved practice feel worse and retain better?
cards.answer: Each attempt forces the pattern to be reconstructed from scratch instead of riding the previous repetition’s momentum. That harder, costlier reconstruction is exactly what drives richer myelination and flexible encoding.

cards.title: Skin Health
cards.prompt: Why does the source prioritise internal optimisation over topical products for skin?
cards.answer: Because skin is a readout, not the system. It sits downstream of gut, sleep and endocrine state, so a topical product treats the display while whatever is generating it continues unchanged.

cards.title: Sleep Architecture
cards.prompt: What distinguishes slow-wave sleep on an EEG?
cards.answer: Synchrony. Hundreds of thousands of cortical neurons fire together and then fall silent together — a level of coordination that occurs in no other physiological state.

cards.title: Sleep Architecture
cards.prompt: What does REM do to an emotionally charged memory?
cards.answer: It replays the memory with norepinephrine suppressed, which strips the emotional charge while preserving the information. The event stays; the physiological reaction to recalling it does not.

cards.title: Sleep Architecture
cards.prompt: What is the evolutionary argument that sleep must be essential?
cards.answer: It is maximally costly — unconscious, paralysed and exposed to predation — and it survived anyway. Nothing that expensive persists unless every alternative arrangement was worse.

cards.title: Sleep Architecture
cards.prompt: Why does cutting two hours off an eight-hour night cost far more than a quarter of your REM?
cards.answer: Because the stages are not evenly distributed. Deep sleep loads the early night and REM the late one, so truncation takes almost all of it from REM — near 100% of slow-wave survives, and perhaps a third of REM.

cards.title: Sleep Architecture
cards.prompt: Why does the brain paralyse the body during REM?
cards.answer: Because it is running at near-waking activity levels. Muscular atonia takes every skeletal muscle offline except the extraocular and inner ear muscles, so the dream cannot be acted out.

cards.title: Sleep Architecture
cards.prompt: Why is sleep efficiency measured separately from sleep duration?
cards.answer: Because time in bed is not time asleep in the right stages. Fragmentation destroys the architecture even when the total looks adequate — 85–90% efficiency is the target, against an 80% average.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: After a bad night, why is sleeping in the wrong move?
cards.answer: It bleeds off the adenosine pressure that would have driven the following night’s sleep — so compensating for one bad night is what manufactures the second.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: What actually produces the afternoon caffeine crash?
cards.answer: Caffeine blocks the adenosine receptors without clearing the adenosine, which keeps accumulating behind the block. When the caffeine clears, all of it reaches the receptors at once.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: What does late caffeine cost you even on a night you fall asleep normally?
cards.answer: Up to 30% of deep slow-wave sleep depth. The EEG architecture shifts, so the glymphatic system never fully activates and you wake unrested despite a full night in bed.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: What does melatonin actually do, if not generate sleep?
cards.answer: It primarily signals circadian timing rather than acting like a conventional sedative. The source reports modest average benefit in healthy adults and argues against assuming that more is better.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: Why can a nap make that night's sleep harder to initiate?
cards.answer: Naps consume adenosine — the same sleep-pressure molecule that has to accumulate through the day to drive nighttime sleep onset.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: Why does a warm shower before bed help, when sleep requires core temperature to drop?
cards.answer: The mechanism is vasodilation, not warming. Warm water pulls blood to the skin surface; stepping into a cooler room then radiates heat away fast, accelerating the 1–2°C core drop that initiates sleep.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: Why does morning light have to be outdoor light, even on an overcast day?
cards.answer: Intensity. Outdoor light on a cloudy day is 10,000–20,000 lux against 100–500 indoors, and the SCN needs the stronger signal to fire the cortisol awakening response and start the countdown to melatonin.

cards.title: Sleep Optimization Protocol
cards.prompt: Why is falling asleep faster after a drink not evidence that alcohol helps sleep?
cards.answer: Because sedation is not sleep — you lost consciousness faster. The brain wave architecture of alcohol-induced unconsciousness differs measurably from natural sleep at every stage.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: How does projection specifically corrupt reading other people?
cards.answer: You run their behaviour through your own emotional grammar. If humour is how you deflect, their humour reads as deflection; if silence meant anger at home, their silence reads as anger.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: What does a mid-conversation spike in blink rate indicate?
cards.answer: A jump in stress or cognitive effort — something shifted internally right then. The useful move is to look back at what was just said rather than at the blinking itself.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: What is the cost of talking constantly, in terms of how you are heard?
cards.answer: Listeners’ brains learn to process your voice as background — you become ambient. Speaking selectively restores the attention, because silence before words signals that what follows was considered.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: Why does the body broadcast discomfort before the conscious mind registers it?
cards.answer: The brain prioritises efficiency over masking, and the signalling systems evolved where emotional transparency was useful — fear needed to show so the tribe could respond.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: Why is accurate reading hardest exactly where it matters most?
cards.answer: Because it requires emotional neutrality, and neutrality is least available when you have something at stake. The generous interpretation gets chosen because the accurate one costs something to accept.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: Why is broken eye contact a poor indicator of lying?
cards.answer: It tracks cognitive load, anxiety and shame far more strongly than deception — and liars, having heard the same myth, tend to increase eye contact to appear credible.

cards.title: Social Signaling
cards.prompt: Why must response latency be read against a personal baseline rather than a standard?
cards.answer: Because the signal is the deviation. A deliberate person pausing tells you nothing; that same person answering at twice their usual speed tells you the topic was already resolved before it was raised.

cards.title: State Cross-Validation
cards.prompt: Why is an idea stronger after state cross-validation?
cards.answer: It has survived both the state that makes possibilities visible and the state that exposes logistical constraints. Endorsement by only one state leaves the other’s information unused.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: What does a credential actually signal, beyond its content?
cards.answer: That you are the kind of person who got through that selection process — conscientiousness and intelligence. It is a costly signal, and the knowledge is close to a side effect.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: What does uptalk signal, and what is the alternative failure mode?
cards.answer: Uptalk — pitch rising at the end of a statement — signals approval-seeking, turning assertions into questions. Monotone fails the other way and signals disengagement; confident speech varies without pleading.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: What is the clearest single status signal, and why does it work?
cards.answer: Comfort in silence. Rushing to fill a gap treats the gap as a failure to be entertaining; tolerating it signals that your value does not depend on this interaction going well.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why can't nonchalance be performed successfully over time?
cards.answer: Performing it requires continuously suppressing the real responses, and the effort of the suppression leaks into the signals. Others’ nervous systems register that something is being held down even when they cannot name it.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why does willingness to disagree make your agreement worth more?
cards.answer: Because agreement inflation has made assent nearly free. Someone who will say “I see it differently” makes their “yes” carry information, which is why calm disagreement increases rather than reduces attention.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why is the informal energy hierarchy in a room often not the official one?
cards.answer: Because the pull goes to whoever is most present, most regulated and least concerned with impressing anyone — which is a different quality from holding the title.

cards.title: Status and Dominance Signals
cards.prompt: Why is the status response automatic rather than a judgement you make?
cards.answer: It runs on an ancient, fast system that evolved when group standing was a survival variable. Listening harder and laughing more readily at a high-status person happens before any conscious decision about them.

cards.title: Stimulus–Response Gap
cards.prompt: What does the stimulus–response gap change without suppressing emotion?
cards.answer: It changes whether the first emotion automatically becomes the public act. The feeling remains input; pausing allows it to be named, contextualised, and answered proportionately.

cards.title: Strategic Adaptation
cards.prompt: What prevents action bias from turning strategic adaptation into escalation?
cards.answer: A stopping rule. Fast execution must be paired with explicit conditions for consolidation, defense, pause, or exit; otherwise the original advantage becomes the reason not to stop.

cards.title: Strategic Understatement
cards.prompt: How can understatement produce more information?
cards.answer: Withholding correction or asking for explanation lets the other person reveal assumptions and reasoning.

cards.title: Strategic Understatement
cards.prompt: What distinction makes strategic understatement possible?
cards.answer: Possessing knowledge or emotion is separate from displaying all of it.

cards.title: Subconscious Reprogramming Methods
cards.prompt: What does successful subconscious reprogramming feel like from the inside?
cards.answer: Not a revelation — a shift in what feels obvious, possible or natural. The default frame updates gradually, so the change registers as the new frame having always been reasonable.

cards.title: Subconscious Reprogramming Methods
cards.prompt: What is offline in theta that is active in beta?
cards.answer: The critical faculty. In beta, incoming information is evaluated, filtered and accepted or rejected; in theta that gate is largely down, which is the state childhood programming was installed through.

cards.title: Subconscious Reprogramming Methods
cards.prompt: Why does waking briefly five hours into sleep open a better theta window than bedtime does?
cards.answer: Re-entering sleep passes through an extended theta phase before dropping to delta. The window is longer and more accessible than the brief hypnagogic slide at the start of the night.

cards.title: Subconscious Reprogramming Methods
cards.prompt: Why does willpower produce change that reverts?
cards.answer: It runs on the 40-bit conscious layer against an 11-million-bit subconscious one that never sleeps. The override works briefly and at cost; when attention depletes, the deeper programming reasserts.

cards.title: Subconscious Reprogramming Methods
cards.prompt: Why must an affirmation be phrased as an identity claim rather than a want?
cards.answer: Because a desire statement encodes the gap. “I want to wake up early” installs the wanting; “I am someone who wakes early” installs the self-concept that would generate the behaviour.

cards.title: Supernormal Stimuli
cards.prompt: On ixcarus's account, what is social media actually farming?
cards.answer: Status, not pleasure — serotonin from validation signals. The system was calibrated for standing inside a tribe of 50–150, so it fires the same way for meaningless engagement from strangers.

cards.title: Supernormal Stimuli
cards.prompt: What did Tinbergen's oversized fake egg demonstrate about evolved recognition?
cards.answer: That an exaggerated version of a natural signal out-triggers the real one — the gull abandons its own egg for the fake. The mechanism has no way to register that it is being exceeded rather than satisfied.

cards.title: Supernormal Stimuli
cards.prompt: Why can you feel physically full and still crave more processed food?
cards.answer: Satiety and desire run on different signals. The homeostatic side registers fullness, while the dopamine side is still responding to a bliss-point stimulus engineered past the range those satiety signals were calibrated against.

cards.title: Supernormal Stimuli
cards.prompt: Why can't real life beat a supernormal stimulus by being better?
cards.answer: The mechanism doing the choosing is not rational — it goes to whatever hits the evolved trigger hardest, and the engineered version always hits harder. Real life only wins once the fake egg is out of reach.

cards.title: Supernormal Stimuli
cards.prompt: Why does short-form video work even when the content is bad?
cards.answer: It exploits novelty detection rather than content quality. The orientation response fires at each new stimulus regardless of what the stimulus is, and a new one arrives every 5–15 seconds.

cards.title: Synaptic Construction
cards.prompt: Why should synaptic construction be separated from myelination?
cards.answer: Establishing and strengthening communication is the foundation; myelination changes transmission efficiency along existing axons. A difficult new response cannot be explained only as an uninsulated finished route.

cards.title: Task–Emotion Mapping
cards.prompt: Why is “use more discipline” a poor generic response to procrastination?
cards.answer: Perfectionism, overwhelm, boredom, outcome anxiety, and genuine misalignment are different predicted costs. One force-based response leaves those distinctions—and therefore the relevant intervention—unknown.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: What was Edison's ball-bearing trick actually detecting?
cards.answer: The border of sleep. Holding the bearings meant that dropping them signalled he had crossed out of hypnagogia into sleep — letting him work the theta window without losing it.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: Why do good ideas arrive in the shower rather than at the desk?
cards.answer: Prefrontal executive control normally directs association toward expected connections. In low-constraint, theta-adjacent states that constraint loosens and associative cortices link across far wider domains.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: Why do parental messages become identity architecture rather than opinions?
cards.answer: They arrive while the child is predominantly in theta and alpha, where the critical filter is not yet operating. Nothing evaluates them, so they are absorbed as structure rather than as claims.

cards.title: Theta State
cards.prompt: Why does trying harder collapse a theta practice?
cards.answer: Effort activates beta, and beta closes the window. The state is held by loose, low-effort awareness — the instruction is to observe and suggest rather than to push.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: How does the kintsugi framing avoid becoming toxic positivity?
cards.answer: It makes no claim that the damage was good. It claims only that the repair can be visible and honoured, and that the repaired self carries a history the unbroken one does not.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: What does a narrow window of tolerance mean in practice?
cards.answer: That inputs a regulated system would process neutrally — a raised voice, an unexpected touch — trigger full threat responses, because the system is calibrated to a historical threat level rather than a present one.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: What is collective or cumulative trauma, as distinct from acute trauma?
cards.answer: ixcarus groups chronic emotional absence, economic stress, inherited scarcity, and isolation as cumulative adversity that may shape regulation. That grouping does not by itself establish trauma or rule PTSD in or out.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: What is titration, and why not simply avoid or flood?
cards.answer: Gradual exposure at a manageable dose. The window of tolerance widens through successful approach — avoidance never tests it, and flooding overwhelms it, so neither expands anything.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: Where does trauma actually reside, if not in the event?
cards.answer: In the sources’ model, an overwhelming response was not integrated, so later cues can reactivate defensive expectations. This is one account of trauma’s persistence, not its complete clinical definition.

cards.title: Trauma and the Nervous System
cards.prompt: Why doesn't knowing where a trauma pattern came from deactivate it?
cards.answer: Because the survival program runs before conscious awareness engages. Insight arrives after the nervous system has already acted, so understanding the origin leaves the physiological program intact.

cards.title: Unstimulated Incubation
cards.prompt: What makes an interval incubation rather than merely downtime?
cards.answer: A prior problem or experience is allowed to remain active while no new high-demand media stream replaces it. Low-demand movement can remain; externally selected input is what is withheld.

cards.title: Validation Seeking
cards.prompt: How does validation-seeking damage the work itself, not just the person?
cards.answer: It swaps the question. “Is this good?” becomes “will this be received well?” — a different question producing different output, and the internal signal that asked the first one atrophies from disuse.

cards.title: Validation Seeking
cards.prompt: What does creating without publishing actually train?
cards.answer: Tolerance of unresolved external uncertainty. Each time approval is absent and nothing bad follows, the nervous system gets evidence against the belief that survival depends on it.

cards.title: Validation Seeking
cards.prompt: Which two neurochemical systems does the posting loop engage at once?
cards.answer: The sources map anticipation to dopamine and the public response to serotonin. Treat that as their explanatory shorthand: uncertain waiting and social evaluation are distinct parts of the loop, even though neither maps exclusively to one chemical.

cards.title: Validation Seeking
cards.prompt: Why does a post with few likes feel worse than neutral?
cards.answer: Public metrics can make social standing feel legible, so low engagement may be experienced as rejection and likes as relief. The source labels this “serotonin farming,” but the behaviour does not reveal a single transmitter directly.

cards.title: Validation Seeking
cards.prompt: Why does heavy social validation leave a person stimulated and lonely at once?
cards.answer: The sources argue that visible engagement can supply stimulation and status feedback without supplying reciprocal intimacy. Their oxytocin language is a metaphorical neurochemical mapping, not a finding that digital connection is biologically empty.

cards.title: Validation Seeking
cards.prompt: Why is validation addiction an adaptation rather than a character flaw?
cards.answer: The sources propose conditional or inconsistent caregiving as one route: approval can become something to earn and monitor. That is a developmental hypothesis, not a diagnosis that can be read directly from adult behaviour.

cards.title: Variable Reward Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What does removing the endpoint from a feed accomplish?
cards.answer: It removes the endpoint of the uncertainty. With no natural stopping cue, the next item is always still a maybe, so the loop has nowhere to resolve.

cards.title: Variable Reward Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour that is hardest to extinguish, and why?
cards.answer: Variable ratio — reward at random, averaging every N actions. The animal can never model when the next one arrives, so there is no point at which the behaviour is safe to stop.

cards.title: Variable Reward Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why can an inconsistent partner produce stronger attachment than a reliably kind one?
cards.answer: Reliability gets modelled and the prediction error falls to zero. Alternating warmth and withdrawal keeps the error machinery firing, so the hypervigilance reads as intensity of feeling when it is a variable reward schedule running.

cards.title: Variable Reward Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why does a maybe produce more dopamine than either a certainty or an impossibility?
cards.answer: Both certainty and impossibility are already modelled, so neither is worth anticipatory resources. Only an uncertain outcome carries information about the environment, and the brain is built to attend hard to exactly that.

cards.title: Variable Reward Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why is anticipating a holiday often better than taking it?
cards.answer: In the sources’ model, anticipation still contains unresolved possibilities, while the experience becomes familiar as it unfolds. That can make anticipation compelling; it does not imply that the experienced reward has no value or dopamine response.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: By this definition, is the house you live in an asset?
cards.answer: In ixcarus’s cash-flow heuristic, an owner-occupied house consumes cash while a rental can produce it. In accounting terms, a residence may still be an asset; the heuristic asks about cash direction rather than replacing the formal category.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: What does leverage actually mean here?
cards.answer: Effort deployed once that keeps paying — code, content and capital all scale without further hours. A job pays once per hour worked; a deployed asset pays indefinitely on a fixed investment.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: Why does starting early beat starting big?
cards.answer: Starting earlier gives returns more periods to compound. It does not guarantee that any small early sum beats any larger later sum; return, duration, fees, and contributions determine the comparison.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: Why does the brain prefer certain mediocrity to uncertain improvement?
cards.answer: In the source’s model, a certain present income feels safer than an uncertain possible improvement. That preference may reflect loss aversion, but the decision must also account for the venture’s real probability and cost of failure.

cards.title: Wealth Systems
cards.prompt: Why is linear income structurally capped regardless of the rate?
cards.answer: It is bounded by a finite, non-renewable input — perhaps ten sustainable working hours a day. A higher hourly rate raises the ceiling without removing it.

cards.title: Adult Neurogenesis
cards.prompt: Why are birth and functional integration different claims in adult neurogenesis?
cards.answer: A new cell can fail to survive or join an active circuit. The source treats production as raw supply and challenging use as part of the process that recruits and retains it.

cards.title: Algorithmic Radicalization
cards.prompt: What changes once a political opinion is held as identity?
cards.answer: A challenge to it stops being a disagreement and becomes an existential threat, which is what licenses dehumanising the person making it.

cards.title: Algorithmic Radicalization
cards.prompt: Which pre-existing feature of attention does the engagement loop exploit?
cards.answer: Negativity bias. Threatening and enraging material already commands disproportionate attention, so an algorithm measuring attention finds anger and keeps supplying it.

cards.title: Algorithmic Radicalization
cards.prompt: Why does optimising for engagement radicalise a user base rather than merely entertain it?
cards.answer: If outrage earns more time and reactions, an engagement objective can select more of it. That can create a radicalizing feedback path, although the metric does not force every feed or user to reach that endpoint.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: What do PTSD triggers, phobias and social anxiety share as a mechanism?
cards.answer: Fear conditioning. A previously neutral stimulus has been associated with threat through experience, so the amygdala now fires on the stimulus rather than on any present danger.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: What is sustaining an emotional reaction past its first ninety seconds?
cards.answer: Re-triggering. The initial neurochemical response runs out on its own; everything after it is thought replaying the trigger and firing the amygdala again.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: Where is the space of agency in an emotional reaction?
cards.answer: The gap between amygdala activation and prefrontal evaluation. A wide gap is emotional intelligence; a narrow one is reactivity — and stress, sleep loss and alcohol narrow it by impairing the prefrontal side.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: Which part of an emotional reaction is available to intervene on?
cards.answer: Not the first ninety seconds — those cannot be prevented. The re-triggering loop can be broken, by physical movement, attention redirection or breathwork.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: Why are emotionally significant events remembered vividly while neutral ones fade?
cards.answer: The amygdala stamps emotional salience onto memory at encoding. Strength of encoding tracks emotional significance rather than importance or accuracy.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: Why does the amygdala read low social status as a survival threat?
cards.answer: Because historically it was one. Exclusion from the tribe meant death, so the machinery that scores status was built on the same alarm as physical danger.

cards.title: Amygdala
cards.prompt: Why was it adaptive for threat detection to run ahead of evaluation?
cards.answer: Because the costs are asymmetric. Fleeing unnecessarily is cheap; evaluating at leisure while being eaten is fatal. Speed was worth the false positives.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: How does convenience produce an inability to motivate oneself?
cards.answer: By removing the resistance the aMCC trains on. Eliminating friction at every point leaves the structure unused, and unused capacity degrades — so the deficit is atrophy, not character.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: What distinguishes embodied discipline from forced discipline?
cards.answer: What is being changed. Forced discipline white-knuckles the same brain structure and regresses when willpower runs out; embodied discipline builds the structure, so the same behaviour costs less each year.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: What is the training stimulus for aMCC growth?
cards.answer: Resistance — the experience of “I don’t want to do this” followed by doing it anyway. The stimulus is the override itself, not the difficulty or the suffering.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: Why does athletic training appear to make people more disciplined outside the gym?
cards.answer: Because the structure it builds is not sport-specific. A larger aMCC transfers to emotional regulation, cognitive persistence and social courage — the “general discipline” is shared infrastructure.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: Why does the type of resistance not matter for aMCC growth?
cards.answer: Because the signal it responds to is overriding the preference for comfort, not the domain the override happens in. A hard conversation and a workout supply the same stimulus.

cards.title: Anterior Midcingulate Cortex (aMCC)
cards.prompt: Why start a resistance protocol with small resistances rather than large ones?
cards.answer: Because the active ingredient is the completed override, and it accrues by reps. A resistance too large to finish supplies no signal — the aMCC responds to progressive overload, like muscle.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: What is dorsal vagal shutdown protecting against, and when did it evolve to fire?
cards.answer: Overwhelming, inescapable threat — the state that follows once fight and flight have both failed. Under chronic unresolvable stress it presents as apathy, which is protection rather than laziness.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: What is the characteristic experience of anhedonia?
cards.answer: Remembering that you liked something while being unable to feel why. The memory of the reward survives; the reward response does not.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: What test distinguishes contentment from managed numbness?
cards.answer: Twenty minutes without stimulation. Genuine calm tolerates stillness; a depleted baseline produces automatic phone reaches and restlessness — the quiet of absence rather than peace.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why can emotional flatness not distinguish apathy from depression by itself?
cards.answer: Apathy names reduced motivation and anhedonia reduced pleasure, while depression can include both. The dimensions overlap rather than forming opposite diagnoses.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why does a working reward system stop registering genuinely good events?
cards.answer: Because it recalibrated rather than broke. Chronic artificial spikes raise the threshold for feeling anything, and ordinary life cannot compete with what the baseline was set against.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why does cutting artificial stimulation make things worse before better?
cards.answer: The spikes were the only input clearing the raised threshold. Removing them leaves nothing registering until the baseline itself falls, so the grey deepens before colour returns.

cards.title: Apathy & Anhedonia
cards.prompt: Why does the recovery protocol put physical inputs before cognitive ones?
cards.answer: Because the nervous system responds to movement, sunlight and cold before it responds to reasoning. Getting the body out of dorsal vagal has to come first — cognition applied to a shut-down system does not land.

cards.title: Aristotle's Three Friendships
cards.prompt: What exactly is the error in a seasonal friendship, if not the friendship itself?
cards.answer: Believing it was permanent while you were in it. The season is fine; the miscategorisation is what leaves you mistaking convenient acquaintances for a social life.

cards.title: Aristotle's Three Friendships
cards.prompt: What is the operational test for which of your friendships are friendships of virtue?
cards.answer: Delete every shared activity and see who still calls. Removing the coffee runs, game nights and gym sessions removes exactly what utility and pleasure friendships were resting on.

cards.title: Aristotle's Three Friendships
cards.prompt: What makes a virtue friendship survive a change of circumstances?
cards.answer: It was never built on the circumstance. It rests on admiring each other’s character, so stripping away every shared activity and reason you met leaves it standing.

cards.title: Aristotle's Three Friendships
cards.prompt: Why do utility and pleasure friendships have an expiry date built in?
cards.answer: They rest on the circumstance rather than the person. When the job, the drinking or the game goes, the thing the friendship was actually made of has gone with it.

cards.title: Artificial vs Natural Reward
cards.prompt: What makes cold exposure and exercise different in shape from a scroll session?
cards.answer: They produce sustained elevation rather than a spike followed by a crash. The dopamine arrives without the debt, which is why they raise baseline instead of borrowing from it.

cards.title: Artificial vs Natural Reward
cards.prompt: What makes junk food and pornography superstimuli rather than ordinary rewards?
cards.answer: They exceed anything the reward system evolved against — palatability beyond any natural food, a sexual signal more intense than any real encounter. The response is calibrated to a signal reality cannot match.

cards.title: Artificial vs Natural Reward
cards.prompt: Where does the dopamine for an artificial spike come from?
cards.answer: The baseline. Recovery from the spike borrows against it, so repeated spiking leaves the resting level chronically depleted and everything unspiked feeling flat.

cards.title: Artificial vs Natural Reward
cards.prompt: Why does an artificial reward require escalation while a natural one does not?
cards.answer: Because it builds no capability, only tolerance. The same input produces a smaller response each time and the dose has to rise; a natural reward’s spike tracks real progress, so what produced it grows too.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: What actually blocks most people from financial independence, if not a low income?
cards.answer: The gap between earned and consumed. Assets can only accumulate out of that difference, so a large income spent entirely builds nothing.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: What structural property caps labour income no matter how well paid it is?
cards.answer: It is sold in hours, and hours are finite. Raising the rate raises the ceiling but does not remove it, and the income stops the moment you do.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: Which property of asset income does labour income lack entirely?
cards.answer: Compounding. Asset income can be reinvested to produce more income; an hour worked produces its wage once and nothing after.

cards.title: Asset vs Labor Income
cards.prompt: Why does a good salary make the job trap harder to leave rather than easier?
cards.answer: Because it makes the trap comfortable. High labour income raises the standard of living the exit would have to be funded past, so the better the wage the more the handcuffs are worth.

cards.title: Attention Economy
cards.prompt: What do infinite scroll and autoplay remove, specifically?
cards.answer: The moment of decision. A book ends and credits roll — those are natural stopping points where continuing has to be chosen. Removing them means the default is always to keep going.

cards.title: Attention Economy
cards.prompt: What does "47 videos watched, 3 remembered" measure?
cards.answer: The extraction rate. Forty-four of those videos left nothing behind — the time was converted into an attention commodity without returning anything to the person who spent it.

cards.title: Attention Economy
cards.prompt: Why does "you are the product" follow from the platform being free?
cards.answer: Because the transaction still has to close. If money is not coming from you, what is being sold is your attention and data — so you are what is delivered to the paying party, not what is served.

cards.title: Attention Economy
cards.prompt: Why is attention time worth more to an advertiser than an impression?
cards.answer: An impression is exposure; sustained attention is engagement that can be measured, targeted and priced. The behavioural data it generates is what makes the next placement more precise.

cards.title: Attention Economy
cards.prompt: Why is willpower the wrong instrument against the attention economy?
cards.answer: The match is not fair. Billion-dollar budgets, behavioural science teams and years of data are optimising against one depleted person with no training in the mechanics. The winning move is changing the structural conditions, not out-resisting the machine.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: What can disclosure change about a physical signal?
cards.answer: Its interpretation. Context can make the same trait look like a byproduct of broader capability or a goal in itself, but disclosure does not change the body or prove that either reading is accurate.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: What is the error in optimising the aesthetic feature directly?
cards.answer: It targets the proxy rather than what the proxy indicates. The detection system is reading health; a surgically produced jawline supplies the shape without the underlying signals it was standing for.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: Why does facial symmetry register as attractive?
cards.answer: It signals developmental stability. Parasites and stress during development produce asymmetry, so symmetry is evidence of a body that grew without those insults.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: Why is posture unusual among the attraction levers?
cards.answer: It changes the hormones as well as the signal, and it costs nothing. Upright open posture raises testosterone and lowers cortisol — so correcting it improves the underlying state, not only the appearance of it.

cards.title: Attraction as Health Signaling
cards.prompt: Why is sleep the highest-impact lever on physical attractiveness?
cards.answer: Because so many separate signals run through it. Skin quality, eye quality, cortisol and therefore testosterone, and hormonal regulation are all downstream of sleep — one input moving several read-outs at once.

cards.title: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor)
cards.prompt: What is the named mechanism connecting aerobic exercise to fluid intelligence?
cards.answer: BDNF. Exercise raises it, it drives neurogenesis and synaptic connection in the hippocampus, and the reasoning gain follows from that — not from mood or general wellbeing.

cards.title: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor)
cards.prompt: What makes the Flynn Effect reversal an opportunity on ixcarus's reading?
cards.answer: Relative position. The average cognitive baseline in developed countries is falling, so holding yours steady through exercise, sleep and nutrition gains ground without any absolute improvement.

cards.title: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor)
cards.prompt: Which brain region does BDNF act on, and why does that region matter?
cards.answer: The hippocampus — the seat of memory formation and spatial reasoning. New neurons surviving there is what turns exercise into better learning rather than only better circulation.

cards.title: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor)
cards.prompt: Why is chronic stress specifically corrosive to learning capacity?
cards.answer: Cortisol suppresses BDNF production and hippocampal function directly. The same structure exercise is building is the one sustained stress degrades.

cards.title: BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor)
cards.prompt: Why schedule cognitive work after exercise rather than before?
cards.answer: Elevated BDNF persists for hours post-exercise. Studying or problem-solving inside that window puts the learning where the plasticity is.

cards.title: Beginner's Mind
cards.prompt: By what mechanism does certainty destroy curiosity?
cards.answer: It withdraws attention. The moment something registers as already known, it stops being looked at — so the knowing is what closes off further noticing.

cards.title: Beginner's Mind
cards.prompt: What do adults arrange their lives to avoid, and what does that cost them?
cards.answer: Doing things they are bad at, because public incompetence is embarrassing. The cost is that they stop entering the state where anything new gets learned at all.

cards.title: Beginner's Mind
cards.prompt: What is the argumentative weight of the convergence across traditions?
cards.answer: That they could not have coordinated. Zen, the Vedas, Rumi, Lao Tzu and the Gospels reach the same posture independently, which is harder to dismiss than any one tradition asserting it.

cards.title: Beginner's Mind
cards.prompt: Why does the beginner see more possibilities than the expert?
cards.answer: The expert’s knowledge has already pruned the options. The beginner assumes they know nothing, so nothing has been ruled out and everything is still worth noticing.

cards.title: Biological Age
cards.prompt: What did the 2023 epigenetic-clock study establish?
cards.answer: That the direction reverses. Around three years of biological age came off in eight weeks via diet, sleep, movement, stress work and supplementation — the size is modest, the reversibility is the finding.

cards.title: Biological Age
cards.prompt: What does subjective age predict, independently of calendar age?
cards.answer: Health, rate of cognitive decline and lifespan. People who genuinely feel younger than their years outperform same-age people who feel every one of them.

cards.title: Biological Age
cards.prompt: What does the Horvath clock actually read?
cards.answer: Chemical marks on DNA. It estimates cellular age from the epigenetic layer, which is why two people of identical calendar age can differ by fifteen or twenty years on it.

cards.title: Biological Age
cards.prompt: Why are the periods of greatest vitality also the periods of fastest ageing?
cards.answer: Because building and maintaining compete. Growth hormone is pro-aging, and the body struggles to do both hard at once — which is why slower development and later puberty track with longer life.

cards.title: Biological Age
cards.prompt: Why does the source call "my prime is behind me" at twenty-nine learned helplessness?
cards.answer: Because it is a belief about uncontrollability applied to the body, and it becomes self-confirming — most people who fall apart swapped training for nostalgia and named the result aging.

cards.title: Biological Age
cards.prompt: Why is there no single number for "your biological age"?
cards.answer: Dozens of clocks run at once and respond to different inputs. The heart can read 28 while the immune system reads 48 on the same passport age.

cards.title: Blackpill
cards.prompt: What premise does the blackpill share with the looksmaxxing community?
cards.answer: That attraction scores fixed individual morphology — bone structure, ratios, angles. They differ only in the conclusion drawn: futility on one side, surgery on the other.

cards.title: Blackpill
cards.prompt: Why does fixed bone structure not make self-improvement futile?
