cards.answer: Because the fixed part is one input among many. The signals attraction reads are spread across dozens of features, and most of them — body composition, hormones, skin quality, posture, movement — respond to effort.

cards.title: Blackpill
cards.prompt: Why does improving several health signals beat perfecting one feature?
cards.answer: The assessment compounds across signals instead of scoring the strongest. Average features on a genuinely healthy body outrank strong features with poor health behind them.

cards.title: Character Under Pressure
cards.prompt: What is the passing response looking for, if not agreeableness?
cards.answer: Preferences with reasons behind them, held without condescension. The test is whether standards track the person’s own values or the price tag of the situation.

cards.title: Character Under Pressure
cards.prompt: Why can a micro-expression not be managed?
cards.answer: Because the emotional response fires before the conscious mind has evaluated whether to show it. The social mask arrives a fraction of a second late, and the face has already broadcast the automatic verdict.

cards.title: Character Under Pressure
cards.prompt: Why does deviation from expectation reveal character when consistency does not?
cards.answer: The prepared presentation only covers the expected case. Once circumstances fall outside it there is no script to run, and what emerges is automatic and unedited.

cards.title: Character Under Pressure
cards.prompt: Why does the method insist on a pattern rather than a single revealing moment?
cards.answer: One unedited response can be a bad day. What predicts is the same reaction recurring across several unrelated deviations, which is what separates character from circumstance.

cards.title: Character Under Pressure
cards.prompt: Why is immediate agreement an ambiguous result on the McDonald's test, not a good one?
cards.answer: It fits two very different people. Genuine ease looks identical to people-pleasing with no centre from the outside, so agreement alone does not distinguish someone comfortable from someone without preferences.

cards.title: Charisma
cards.prompt: What does each two-out-of-three combination of presence, power and warmth produce?
cards.answer: Warmth without power is likeable but not influential; power without warmth is respected but not approached; presence without either is forgettable. All three are load-bearing.

cards.title: Charisma
cards.prompt: What is "power" in the charisma model, given that it is not dominance?
cards.answer: Not needing the interaction to go a particular way in order to be okay. It is the behaviour of operating from abundance rather than requiring validation from the exchange.

cards.title: Charisma
cards.prompt: What is the observable tell that warmth is genuine rather than performed?
cards.answer: A follow-up question that could not have been prepared in advance. It is evidence the listening actually happened, which complimenting and enthusiasm are not.

cards.title: Charisma
cards.prompt: Why does rushing to fill a silence read as low status?
cards.answer: Because it shows the interaction is needed. Tolerating silence signals that nothing is riding on the exchange going a particular way, which is the whole content of the power signal.

cards.title: Charisma
cards.prompt: Why is a well-executed social script forgettable?
cards.answer: Because the brain compresses predictable patterns into almost nothing. A recognisable script gets categorised and filed on sight; only a departure from the expected pattern gets stored.

cards.title: Charisma
cards.prompt: Why is full presence compelling rather than merely polite?
cards.answer: Because it is rare. Most people are half-present at best, so undivided attention registers as a safety signal and reads as “you matter right now” — scarcity is doing the work.

cards.title: Cognitive Performance Phases
cards.prompt: What does a Pavlovian work anchor actually buy?
cards.answer: Transition time. Pairing a fixed set of cues with deep work trains the brain to enter the state on the cue, compressing the on-ramp from 20–30 minutes to a few.

cards.title: Cognitive Performance Phases
cards.prompt: What is the real cost of doing email first thing in the morning?
cards.answer: It spends the peak window. The 2–4 hours after the cortisol awakening response carry the day’s best executive function and working memory, and that capacity does not come back later.

cards.title: Cognitive Performance Phases
cards.prompt: What produces the feeling of being busy all day without being productive?
cards.answer: Mismatched supply and demand. Deep work placed in a low-signal phase takes several times longer and comes out worse, so the hours are spent without the output appearing.

cards.title: Cognitive Performance Phases
cards.prompt: Why does an irregular wake time cost more than the lost sleep itself?
cards.answer: The phases are anchored to the cortisol awakening response. An unpredictable wake time leaves you unable to place work against them, and flattens the peak’s intensity as well.

cards.title: Cognitive Performance Phases
cards.prompt: Why is the fix for the 9pm collapse structural rather than motivational?
cards.answer: Because the resource is genuinely gone — working memory, decision quality and impulse control are measurably reduced, not merely unwilling. Motivation cannot restore a depleted pool; moving the work earlier avoids needing it.

cards.title: Comfort Compounding
cards.prompt: Comfort compounding moves two quantities in opposite directions. Which?
cards.answer: The cost of leaving rises — lifestyle, obligations, identity investment — while the capacity to leave falls, as skills go undeveloped and risk tolerance goes unmaintained. The gap widens from both ends.

cards.title: Comfort Compounding
cards.prompt: In what sense is "I can't take that risk now" literally true after years of comfort?
cards.answer: The tolerance is a physical capacity that has degraded. The aMCC shrinks without resistance, so the deficit is in handling the discomfort of the risk, not in the size of the risk itself.

cards.title: Comfort Compounding
cards.prompt: What makes comfort compound rather than merely accumulate?
cards.answer: Each day’s avoidance changes the conditions for the next one — the situation entrenches and the capacity degrades, so the following day’s avoidance is easier. It is the same non-linear mathematics as growth, run in reverse.

cards.title: Comfort Compounding
cards.prompt: Why introduce resistance before it feels necessary?
cards.answer: Because by the time it feels necessary the capacity to act on it has degraded. Intervening early means rebuilding from mild atrophy rather than from a state where the required exit already feels impossible.

cards.title: Comfort Zone
cards.prompt: What is discomfort actually signalling, on this account?
cards.answer: That neuroplasticity is occurring — the current neural configuration is being challenged and something is building. Avoiding the feeling means avoiding the only contexts where growth happens.

cards.title: Comfort Zone
cards.prompt: Which two chemicals gate neuroplasticity, and what triggers them?
cards.answer: Norepinephrine and acetylcholine — alertness and focused attention. Both are released by genuine challenge and novelty at the edge of current capability, which is why comfortable practice does not rewire anything.

cards.title: Comfort Zone
cards.prompt: Why is "staying the same" not actually a stable state?
cards.answer: Because reinforcement is relative. The comfortable pathways keep getting myelinated while the difficulty-handling ones do not, so holding position is a slow loss of the capacity you are not using.

cards.title: Comfort Zone
cards.prompt: Why is the cage hard to see while it is being built?
cards.answer: Because every individual bar is a reasonable choice. This job is safe enough, this relationship good enough to not risk — no single decision looks like a mistake, and the structure only appears in aggregate.

cards.title: Compound Effect
cards.prompt: After five years of 1% worse daily decisions, what has actually changed?
cards.answer: Repeated choices can change attention, skill, environment, and the ease of the next choice. The sources add aMCC and myelination explanations, but a five-year behavioural history does not by itself reveal measured brain-volume changes.

cards.title: Compound Effect
cards.prompt: What error do people make in the invisible growth phase?
cards.answer: Reading no visible progress as no progress. The foundation is accumulating the whole time; what is missing is the threshold at which it becomes observable.

cards.title: Compound Effect
cards.prompt: What is an "overnight success", in the bucket analogy?
cards.answer: The overflow moment. The pouring was outpacing the drain for a long time before the water became visible above the rim — the visible event is the last part of a long process, not the process.

cards.title: Compound Effect
cards.prompt: Why can you not tell the improving person from the declining one early on?
cards.answer: The graphs have not diverged yet. Exponential curves are nearly flat and nearly identical near the origin, so the difference in direction is real long before it is visible.

cards.title: Compound Effect
cards.prompt: Why start absurdly small if the goal is a large result?
cards.answer: Because what is being established early is trajectory, not performance. Magnitude comes from the exponent; the only thing that has to be right at the start is the direction and the fact that it repeats.

cards.title: Compound Effect
cards.prompt: Why track behaviours rather than results in the early phase?
cards.answer: Because outcomes are uninformative there. In the flat part of the curve the results cannot distinguish a working process from a failing one, while the behaviours can.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: Cortisol supports testosterone in the morning but suppresses it chronically. What does that distinction turn on?
cards.answer: Acute versus sustained elevation. A short morning surge is supportive; keeping cortisol up through the day — which late caffeine does — flips the effect.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: What does early morning light do that makes it high leverage at zero cost?
cards.answer: Two things at once: it anchors the circadian rhythm and triggers the cortisol awakening response. One free input sets both the day’s timing and its alertness.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: Why are eight hours at a random time not equivalent to eight hours at a fixed one?
cards.answer: The circadian system responds to consistency, not duration alone. Irregular timing disrupts cortisol timing, sleep architecture and the alertness window even when the total is adequate.

cards.title: Cortisol Awakening Response
cards.prompt: Why delay caffeine roughly two hours after waking?
cards.answer: Because the cortisol awakening response is already supplying alertness. Caffeine taken into it compounds rather than complements, and the larger combined peak makes the later crash worse.

cards.title: Curiosity Gap
cards.prompt: What makes withheld information hold attention better than complete information?
cards.answer: It leaves an open loop. Incomplete information stays cognitively active and demands closure, whereas a resolved story can be set down.

cards.title: Curiosity Gap
cards.prompt: Why can anticipation motivate more strongly than the reward it points at?
cards.answer: The dopamine response arrives before resolution. The wanting is the chemically active part, so an unopened promise can pull harder than whatever is eventually inside it.

cards.title: Curiosity Gap
cards.prompt: Why does labelling something "banned" raise its perceived value?
cards.answer: Because restriction raises perceived value regardless of content. The label is doing the work — nothing about the material itself has to change for it to become more attractive.

cards.title: Curiosity Gap
cards.prompt: Why is a vague threat more effective than a specific one?
cards.answer: Because it cannot be checked or dismissed, and the mind fills the gap with its own worst version. A specific claim can be verified and closed; an unnamed one stays open indefinitely.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: What does Alexander having no answer to "what comes after conquering everything" expose?
cards.answer: That the goal was never terminal. A project justified by proving you are the greatest has no completion condition, so finishing it leaves nothing behind it.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: What does Diogenes throwing away his cup demonstrate?
cards.answer: That a possession can be revealed as unnecessary by a single counterexample. The cup had seemed like a minimum; a child drinking from cupped hands showed it was baggage.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: What is the modern Cynic critique, stated without the jar?
cards.answer: That the objects being worked for mostly exist to be seen by other people. Forty years are traded for a house rarely occupied and a car whose function is to signal to strangers.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: Where does Cynicism locate freedom?
cards.answer: In wanting less, not in acquiring more. The route to it is subtraction of artificial convention rather than accumulation against it.

cards.title: Cynicism
cards.prompt: Why would the most powerful man alive envy a man who owned nothing?
cards.answer: Because Diogenes already had what the conquest was for. Alexander was chasing freedom through acquisition and remained bound to being seen as great; Diogenes had reached it by needing nothing.

cards.title: Dark Motivation
cards.prompt: What separates dark motivation from shame-based motivation?
cards.answer: Where the claim points. “I will not be that” is about a future to avoid and produces movement; “I am that” is about a present identity and produces freeze.

cards.title: Dark Motivation
cards.prompt: Why can dark motivation not be borrowed from someone else?
cards.answer: Its force comes from being personally charged — fear, anger or shame attached to something specific in your own history. Someone else’s version is intellectually understandable and therefore inert.

cards.title: Dark Motivation
cards.prompt: Why is dark motivation described as kindling rather than fuel?
cards.answer: It is only needed until the fire catches. Once the behaviour is myelinated and identity has shifted, it runs without the emotional charge — and sustaining that charge indefinitely is exhausting and counterproductive.

cards.title: Dark Motivation
cards.prompt: Why is the early phase of a behaviour change the most expensive?
cards.answer: Myelination has not begun, so nothing about the behaviour runs automatically. Every repetition costs full willpower against maximal resistance — the demand is highest exactly when the infrastructure is absent.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What is the most reliable detection signal, given that the behaviour itself may look fine?
cards.answer: Your own state. Feeling consistently confused, diminished or off-balance around someone — and clearer and more capable away from them — is data the constructed mask cannot suppress.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What is the primary protection against dark triad dynamics?
cards.answer: Walk-away power. The leverage comes from your dependence on the relationship, so having a real alternative is worth more than detecting any individual tactic.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What makes gaslighting self-reinforcing at the neurological level?
cards.answer: The stress it creates degrades hippocampal memory reliability via cortisol. The resulting confusion is then presented as proof that your perception was the problem all along.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: What separates Machiavellianism from narcissism in what drives the behaviour?
cards.answer: Narcissism is driven by emotional need — a fragile self-image requiring propping up. Machiavellianism is driven by strategic advantage, with people treated as instruments rather than as validators.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: Why do dark triad profiles come across as unusually charming at first?
cards.answer: Fewer internal inhibitions read as confidence, and the mask has been deliberately constructed for impact. What looks like natural ease is the absence of the hesitation most people have.

cards.title: Dark Triad
cards.prompt: Why is a Machiavellian the hardest of the three to detect at work?
cards.answer: Because the behaviour is genuinely rational and cooperative right up until cooperation stops serving the goal. There is no emotional volatility to notice in advance.

cards.title: Decision Fatigue
cards.prompt: What does the parole study establish that a simple "judges get tired" claim does not?
cards.answer: That the outcome tracked position in the day rather than the case. Comparably similar cases were decided differently depending on when they arrived, and the rate recovered after meal breaks.

cards.title: Decision Fatigue
cards.prompt: What is a fixed routine actually buying, on this account?
cards.answer: Cognitive budget. Removing low-value decisions from the morning leaves the finite capacity intact for the decisions that deserve it — the point is not rigidity.

cards.title: Decision Fatigue
cards.prompt: What shows that evening exhaustion after office work is not physical?
cards.answer: Sufficient incentive would still get a couple of miles out of the body. The capacity that is genuinely gone is the decision-making one, spent on dozens of small unplanned choices through the day.

cards.title: Decision Fatigue
cards.prompt: Why stage the environment the night before rather than rely on morning intention?
cards.answer: Because discipline is at its lowest on waking. Decisions made the previous evening, when capacity was available, are decisions the morning does not have to fund.

cards.title: Default Mode Network (DMN)
cards.prompt: What is boredom signalling, neurologically?
cards.answer: That the brain has processed its current inputs and is ready to enter DMN mode. Filling it immediately interrupts the synthesis the signal was announcing.

cards.title: Default Mode Network (DMN)
cards.prompt: Why does intermittent stimulation block the DMN specifically?
cards.answer: The network needs a baseline quiet to enter. Unpredictable stimulation holds the brain in a low-grade alert state, which never clears the threshold the DMN requires.

cards.title: Default Mode Network (DMN)
cards.prompt: Why is calling the default mode network "the brain doing nothing" wrong?
cards.answer: It is a different mode of computation, not an absence of one — memory consolidation, creative synthesis, self-referential processing, social cognition and future planning all run there.

cards.title: Default Mode Network (DMN)
cards.prompt: Why might the quiet person in a meeting be doing more cognitive work than the loud one?
cards.answer: Silence permits DMN activation, where connections across domains are made. The register differs from verbal debate rather than the quantity of thought being lower.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What distinguishes projection from ordinary dislike?
cards.answer: The intensity. Mild dislike is preference; disproportionate, specific rage is recognition — the trait is being seen rather than merely disliked.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What does a defence mechanism do to a conflict?
cards.answer: Moves it out of sight, not out of existence. The conflict keeps running below consciousness — what changes is your access to it, not its activity.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: What is the ordering that makes rationalisation a defence rather than reasoning?
cards.answer: The decision came first and the logic after. The explanation is manufactured to cover an emotional outcome already reached, which is why it always arrives fully formed and always favours the same conclusion.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why is repression more dangerous than a memory you can still reach?
cards.answer: Because it keeps its influence while losing its address. The buried moment still decides how you flinch and still runs the relationships, but there is no longer anything conscious to trace the behaviour back to.

cards.title: Defense Mechanisms
cards.prompt: Why is the serial cheater convinced his partner is cheating?
cards.answer: He is projecting his own model outward. He knows how easy it is, so he assumes everyone runs the same game — describing himself while pointing at her.

cards.title: Delayed Gratification
cards.prompt: How did previous generations train delay tolerance without intending to?
cards.answer: The infrastructure had no alternative. Hunting, farming, letters and saving all imposed a gap between effort and reward, so the capacity was built as a by-product of ordinary life rather than as a practice.

cards.title: Delayed Gratification
cards.prompt: What is the dopamine baseline calibrated to, beyond the size of a reward?
cards.answer: The speed of delivery it experiences most often. Calibrated to instant reward, anything requiring a wait registers as abnormal and produces distress.

cards.title: Delayed Gratification
cards.prompt: What is the pathological form of delayed gratification?
cards.answer: Indefinite deferral — never allowing the reward, with satisfaction always saved for a future moment that keeps moving. Delay substituted for achievement rather than serving it.

cards.title: Delayed Gratification
cards.prompt: Why does finishing projects rebuild delay tolerance specifically?
cards.answer: Because completion is the rep. Each finished project is one full effort-before-reward cycle survived, which is the exposure the recalibration requires — abandoning at the interesting part never supplies it.

cards.title: Delayed Gratification
cards.prompt: Why is delay tolerance the precondition for compound growth specifically?
cards.answer: Because compounding pays nothing visible in its early phase. Reaching the curve requires sustained investment through a stretch where results are absent, which is exactly what delay intolerance cannot survive.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice
cards.prompt: What goes wrong in practice without immediate feedback?
cards.answer: The learner cannot locate the prediction error, so the next attempt has no reason to change. Repetition can then stabilize the same mistake instead of correcting it.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice
cards.prompt: Why does a skill practised well sometimes fail entirely under real conditions?
cards.answer: Because what was practised was a performance of the routine in predictable, low-stress conditions, not the underlying capability. Nothing in that practice covered the variability the real setting supplies.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice
cards.prompt: Why does twenty years of experience not automatically beat two?
cards.answer: Because naive practice stops improving anything once competence is reached. Repeating what you can already do maintains performance; only practice beyond current ability moves it.

cards.title: Deliberate Practice
cards.prompt: Why does unstructured practice drift toward strengths?
cards.answer: Because it is comfortable and it feels like competence. The pull is toward what already works, which is exactly the material that has nothing left to teach.

cards.title: Derealization
cards.prompt: How does the source distinguish derealization from ordinary distraction?
cards.answer: Attention is not merely elsewhere; the whole scene loses felt immediacy, as though information is being processed across a membrane rather than inhabited as experience.

cards.title: Detachment & Letting Go
cards.prompt: How does attachment to an outcome distort the behaviour aimed at it?
cards.answer: It shifts optimisation onto the metric instead of onto what produces the metric. Effort goes to subscriber count rather than to the writing quality that earns subscribers.

cards.title: Detachment & Letting Go
cards.prompt: What is the nervous-system account of why detachment improves results?
cards.answer: Attachment holds the system in sympathetic threat-monitoring; detachment reduces the monitoring load and permits a calmer parasympathetic state. Releasing the outcome leaves more attention available for the input that can actually be improved.

cards.title: Detachment & Letting Go
cards.prompt: What separates detachment from indifference?
cards.answer: Where the investment goes, not how much there is. Indifference is low investment everywhere; detachment is maximum investment in what is controllable and none in managing what is not.

cards.title: Detachment & Letting Go
cards.prompt: Why does neediness reliably repel in relationships?
cards.answer: The qualities that attract — presence, self-sufficiency, absorption in purpose — are exactly what anxious monitoring of another person’s validation consumes. The pursuit spends the thing being pursued with.

cards.title: Digital Addiction
cards.prompt: What is the relationship between platform design and addiction science?
cards.answer: The same research base, applied in reverse. Behavioural scientists who could be reducing compulsive use are instead employed to maximise it.

cards.title: Digital Addiction
cards.prompt: What makes phone-checking compulsive rather than merely habitual?
cards.answer: It often fires before the conscious mind has decided to check. The cue-response loop runs on its own, so the decision to reach for the device happens after the reach.

cards.title: Digital Addiction
cards.prompt: Which four clinical criteria does phone use actually meet?
cards.answer: Tolerance, withdrawal, compulsive use, and continued use despite harm. The word is not being used loosely — the same four markers that define substance addiction are present.

cards.title: Digital Addiction
cards.prompt: Why is an unpredictable feed more compelling than a reliably good one?
cards.answer: Because dopamine fires on anticipation rather than on the reward. A predictable reward resolves the anticipation; an unpredictable one keeps it running, which is what produces compulsive checking.

cards.title: Dominance vs. Prestige
cards.prompt: What are the neurochemical signatures of high and low status?
cards.answer: High status runs on dopamine and serotonin — forward motivation, calm, assertiveness. Low status runs on cortisol with reduced testosterone — anxiety, vigilance, submission.

cards.title: Dominance vs. Prestige
cards.prompt: What does the barista example establish about where power comes from?
cards.answer: Control over a desired resource, not organisational rank. The same executive who outranks everyone in the building has none of it in a domain where he has to defer.

cards.title: Dominance vs. Prestige
cards.prompt: What is the common failure mode of reaching for dominance signals?
cards.answer: Projecting authority with no competence substrate beneath it. It holds briefly, then fails publicly — and the public failure costs more social capital than never claiming the status would have.

cards.title: Dominance vs. Prestige
cards.prompt: What test distinguishes prestige from dominance?
cards.answer: Removing the formal authority. Prestige survives it — people still seek the person out — because it rested on demonstrated competence rather than on the capacity to impose costs.

cards.title: Dominance vs. Prestige
cards.prompt: Why is dominance-based status inherently unstable?
cards.answer: It exists only while the threat capacity is perceived. Remove, weaken or successfully challenge the individual and the compliance ends — often with backlash, because nothing was freely given.

cards.title: Dominance vs. Prestige
cards.prompt: Why is the ability to walk away the most durable source of leverage?
cards.answer: Because it does not depend on anyone’s perception of you. Anyone who cannot afford to lose you cannot control you, and real alternatives are yours whether or not they are recognised.

cards.title: Dopamine Hijacking
cards.prompt: What accounts for a child's wonder at a puddle, on this account?
cards.answer: Calibration, not innocence. A dopamine system set against subtle natural rewards finds them sufficient — the wonder is what an uncorrupted baseline produces.

cards.title: Dopamine Hijacking
cards.prompt: What distinguishes dopamine hijacking from the hedonic treadmill, given both are baseline drift?
cards.answer: What the baseline adapts to. The hedonic treadmill tracks achievement levels; dopamine hijacking tracks stimulation intensity. The escalation logic is identical.

cards.title: Dopamine Hijacking
cards.prompt: Why does the early stage of a digital detox feel like withdrawal?
cards.answer: Because the raised baseline is still in place. Nothing available is clearing the threshold the system has been calibrated to, and the demand for the usual spike does not fall as fast as the input does.

cards.title: Dopamine Hijacking
cards.prompt: Why does the natural world start feeling grey after heavy screen use?
cards.answer: Nothing about the world changed — the baseline expectation of stimulation rose. Screens deliver saturation and novelty beyond anything natural, and the adapted system reads ordinary input as falling short.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: What is receptor downregulation, and what triggers it?
cards.answer: The brain cutting receptor count and sensitivity to compensate for chronic overstimulation. It is a protective adjustment to too much signal, and it is what drops the baseline.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: What is the goal of recalibration, if not zero stimulation?
cards.answer: A narrower spike range. The baseline can only stabilise if the peaks stop overshooting it — variance, not abstinence, is the target.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: Why does swapping social media for Netflix change nothing?
cards.answer: The baseline responds to spike magnitude, not to the source. Substituting one high-intensity input for another keeps the threshold exactly where it was.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: Why does the baseline drop further in the first days of recalibration?
cards.answer: The downregulated receptors are still downregulated while the input that was compensating for them is gone. Recovery of sensitivity lags the removal of the spikes, which is why days 2–5 are the hardest.

cards.title: Dopamine Recalibration
cards.prompt: Why is "dopamine detox" the wrong name for the process?
cards.answer: Dopamine cannot be eliminated — it is not a toxin to clear. What is being restored is baseline sensitivity, by narrowing the spike range rather than removing the neurotransmitter.

cards.title: Dopaminergic System
cards.prompt: What does it mean that an artificial spike "borrows from baseline"?
cards.answer: The elevation is repaid during recovery. Chronic spiking therefore leaves a chronically depleted baseline, raising the threshold at which anything registers as pleasurable at all.

cards.title: Dopaminergic System
cards.prompt: What shifts in the dopamine signal once a habit is encoded?
cards.answer: Its timing. Initially the reward produces the dopamine; after encoding the cue does, firing anticipation before the behaviour — which is why the behaviour stops needing a decision.

cards.title: Dopaminergic System
cards.prompt: Which dopamine pathway fails first when the baseline is depleted, and what does it cost?
cards.answer: The mesocortical pathway, running from the VTA to the prefrontal cortex. Its job is executive function and focus, so depletion shows up as an inability to concentrate rather than as low mood.

cards.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect
cards.prompt: What does overwhelming confidence about a complex domain actually signal?
cards.answer: Possible early-curve positioning. Certainty is cheapest before the depth is visible, so unqualified confidence is weak evidence of expertise and moderate evidence against it.

cards.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect
cards.prompt: What is the mechanism behind beginners overrating themselves?
cards.answer: You cannot know what you don’t know. Surface exposure supplies no view of the territory beneath it, so the beginner’s estimate of the whole is built from the only part they can see.

cards.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect
cards.prompt: Why does expertise produce silence as a by-product?
cards.answer: The expert knows the size of what they do not know, and has been wrong often enough to wait for something worth saying. The beginner is unaware of the questions they cannot answer, so nothing stops them talking.

cards.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect
cards.prompt: Why does the valley of despair feel like failure when it is progress?
cards.answer: Because the gap between perceived and required competence is at its widest there. The subjective signal — I am worse at this than I thought — is exactly what an accurate first look at the domain produces.

cards.title: Dunning-Kruger Effect
cards.prompt: Why is confidence lowest at the point where understanding is advancing fastest?
cards.answer: Because the gap has just become visible. Knowing enough to see how much is missing lowers the estimate of your competence at exactly the moment it is actually improving.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: What counts as "cost" in the brain's pricing of a task?
cards.answer: Uncertainty, fear of failure, social judgment, ambiguity, cognitive effort and emotional discomfort — not only physical exertion. That is why two physically identical tasks can price completely differently.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: What happens to motivation when perceived cost exceeds expected reward?
cards.answer: It disappears rather than diminishing. The calculation is not a dial that turns down — losing it flips the task to not worth starting, which is why willing yourself into it does not work.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: What is the operational question to ask about a task you keep failing to start?
cards.answer: How many decisions stand between you and beginning. “Put shoes on and go” hides finding clothes, charging headphones, choosing a playlist, deciding the workout — each one a real cost.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: Why can one email feel impossible while forty-five minutes of scrolling is effortless?
cards.answer: Identical physical demand, opposite prices. The scroll carries no uncertainty or judgment; the email carries both, and the brain prices what you do not consciously see.

cards.title: Effort-Cost Calculation
cards.prompt: Why do high performers wear identical clothes and keep fixed routines?
cards.answer: To remove decisions from the path, not to display discipline. If the friction is low enough the decision never has to be made, so motivation never has to cover it.

cards.title: Ego
cards.prompt: How does the universal-selfishness claim absorb humility as a counterexample?
cards.answer: By locating the ego in the identity rather than the act. Being known as someone without an ego is itself something the ego can be invested in, so the apparent exception is the claim operating one level up.

cards.title: Ego
cards.prompt: What does it mean to channel the ego productively rather than suppress it?
cards.answer: Satisfying the drive through the real thing instead of the appearance. Wanting to feel superior becomes becoming genuinely good at something valuable; wanting to feel important becomes doing important work.

cards.title: Ego
cards.prompt: Why does an appeal to self-interest outperform an appeal to altruism?
cards.answer: Because it addresses the actual motivation rather than the stated one. Framing the request as something that serves them removes the need for them to be generous in order to agree.

cards.title: Ego
cards.prompt: Why is the openly selfish person less dangerous than the performed altruist?
cards.answer: Because the game is visible. Both are serving the ego; only one is also denying it, and the denial removes the information you would need to price the interaction.

cards.title: Ego Games
cards.prompt: How do you locate your own ego investments?
cards.answer: By what you defend hardest under criticism. The intensity of the protection marks where the investment is, more reliably than any account you would give of yourself.

cards.title: Ego Games
cards.prompt: What determines whether validation or challenge lands, on this account?
cards.answer: Not whether either is correct. Validation generates loyalty and challenge generates defensiveness regardless of validity, because the response is to the ego position rather than to the argument.

cards.title: Ego Games
cards.prompt: What is the practical consequence of not seeing the ego games?
cards.answer: You are still playing them, without agency. The dynamics operate whether or not they are noticed — the choice is between navigating them and being navigated by them.

cards.title: Ego Games
cards.prompt: Why does asking for advice generate more cooperation than asking for help?
cards.answer: Advice positions the other person as an expert; help positions them as a resource. The first feeds the ego game, the second spends it.

cards.title: Ego Games
cards.prompt: Why does not needing to win the ego games confer the strongest social position?
cards.answer: Because ego need is the handle other people use. Someone who does not require recognition or validation offers nothing to trade against — which makes them both less manipulable and more trustworthy.

cards.title: Emotional Intelligence
cards.prompt: How can displayed intelligence cancel its own advantage?
cards.answer: By triggering threat response, jealousy and defensiveness in others. The capability is real, but the social reaction closes off the cooperation and information that would let it be used.

cards.title: Emotional Intelligence
cards.prompt: What distinguishes guilt from shame as signals?
cards.answer: Whose standard was breached. Guilt marks a violation of your own values; shame marks a violation of others’ expectations — so they call for different responses.

cards.title: Emotional Intelligence
cards.prompt: What does a reaction disproportionate to its trigger tell you?
cards.answer: That the trigger is not the source. Proportionate reactions are about the present situation; excessive ones are biographical, and responding to the surface content addresses the wrong thing.

cards.title: Emotional Intelligence
cards.prompt: What information does envy carry?
cards.answer: What you actually want. Envy is a read-out of your own preferences, arriving from a source that has less incentive to flatter you than deliberate reflection does.

cards.title: Emotional Intelligence
cards.prompt: What makes a regulated person feel magnetic rather than merely pleasant?
cards.answer: Co-regulation. Their nervous system state transfers — cortisol drops, breathing slows, voice relaxes in the people around them — so the effect is a physiological change rather than an impression.

cards.title: Emotional Intelligence
cards.prompt: Why does suppressing an emotion cost more than regulating it?
cards.answer: Suppression has to be maintained. It consumes ongoing resources, raises cortisol, leaks through signals it cannot fully mask, and erupts amplified when it fails — where a regulated emotion completes its cycle and releases the resources.

cards.title: Endocrine Disruptors
cards.prompt: Why are the page’s exposure-reduction suggestions not a treatment protocol?
cards.answer: The cited sources do not establish population effects or treatment outcomes for those recommendations.

cards.title: Endocrine Disruptors
cards.prompt: Why is “the body cannot tell the difference” too crude for endocrine disruptors?
cards.answer: A compound may activate, block or alter feedback differently by tissue and dose.

cards.title: Energy Management
cards.prompt: What does context switching actually cost, beyond the interruption itself?
cards.answer: The reload. Each switch forces the brain to rebuild the context it had already assembled, so the cost is paid again every time regardless of how brief the departure was.

cards.title: Energy Management
cards.prompt: Why is protecting energy a precondition for learning, not just for output?
cards.answer: Because consolidation happens in rest. A schedule that leaves no unspent capacity removes the phase in which what was practised actually gets encoded.

cards.title: Energy Management
cards.prompt: Why treat energy rather than time as the primary planning unit?
cards.answer: Because time on a depleted system produces nothing. Hours are only convertible into output at the rate the available energy allows, which makes energy the binding constraint.

cards.title: Epicureanism
cards.prompt: How does Epicurus define pleasure, and why does that reverse the popular reading?
cards.answer: As the absence of physical pain and mental anxiety, not the presence of indulgence. Defined negatively, more consumption does not produce more pleasure — which makes the philosophy austere rather than hedonistic.

cards.title: Epicureanism
cards.prompt: What are Epicurus's three classes of desire?
cards.answer: Natural and necessary (food, water, shelter); natural but unnecessary (fine food, wine, small luxuries); and unnatural and unnecessary (wealth, fame, power) — the last being the desires that never fill up.

cards.title: Epicureanism
cards.prompt: What distinguishes the third class of desire from the second?
cards.answer: That it has no satiation point. Fine wine is pleasant and finishable; wealth, fame and power never fill up no matter how much is poured in.

cards.title: Epicureanism
cards.prompt: What is the Epicurean argument against fearing death?
cards.answer: That you and it never coexist. While you exist, death is not present; when death is present, you are not — so there is no moment at which the thing feared is experienced.

cards.title: Epicureanism
cards.prompt: Why is excess self-defeating on Epicurean terms rather than merely immoral?
cards.answer: Because pleasure was defined as the absence of pain. Gluttony produces the sickness and chasing every craving wrecks the tranquility — the indulgence destroys the very state it was meant to produce.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: If DNA is the music, what is the epigenome?
cards.answer: The reader deciding which songs play in which cell. Every cell holds the same score; the epigenome is what makes a liver cell play liver music and a neuron play neuron music.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: On Sinclair's model, what is ageing fundamentally?
cards.answer: A loss of information, not wear on parts. The instructions for which genes play in which cell degrade like a photocopy of a photocopy, and cells begin losing their identity.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: What goes wrong in a cell when the epigenetic reader is scratched?
cards.answer: Genes that should stay silent switch on and genes that should be playing shut off. The cell starts behaving like something other than what it is.

cards.title: Epigenome
cards.prompt: Why is "your DNA is not your fate" a claim about leverage rather than optimism?
cards.answer: Because roughly 80% of future health and longevity sits in the epigenetic layer rather than the genes. The sequence is fixed; the reader is influenceable daily, so almost all the movable weight is on the modifiable side.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: How does chronic stress worsen estrogen dominance?
cards.answer: By suppressing progesterone, the hormone that balances estrogen in the luteal phase. Chemical exposure raises the estrogen signal from one side while cortisol removes the counterweight from the other.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Which organ governs estrogen clearance, and why does that make it a lever?
cards.answer: The liver. When it is overloaded, clearance slows and the signal accumulates — so supporting its metabolism, via indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables, acts on the exit rather than the entrance.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Why can estrogen dominance occur without elevated estrogen?
cards.answer: Because receptors are finite and xenoestrogens compete for them. What is dominant is the estrogen-like signalling, which a blood concentration of real estrogen does not capture.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Why can excessive high-intensity cardio work against hormonal balance?
cards.answer: It spikes cortisol enough to suppress reproductive hormones. The exercise is not the problem; the cortisol load from too much of the high-intensity kind is, which is why moderate volume is prescribed.

cards.title: Estrogen Dominance
cards.prompt: Why does cutting dietary fat too far undermine sex hormone production?
cards.answer: Estrogen and progesterone are built from cholesterol. Below roughly 25–30% of calories from fat, the raw material for synthesis is missing.

cards.title: Eternal Recurrence
cards.prompt: What does an affirmative answer to the recurrence test not require?
cards.answer: Liking every event or endorsing every harm.

cards.title: Eternal Recurrence
cards.prompt: What is eternal recurrence used as on this page?
cards.answer: A diagnostic test of present choices, not a literal prediction about the universe.

cards.title: Eudaimonia
cards.prompt: What did Aristotle get right that required brain scanners to confirm?
cards.answer: That repeated action physically becomes identity. Myelination of a rehearsed pathway is the mechanism he had no access to, and he reached the conclusion by observation alone.

cards.title: Eudaimonia
cards.prompt: What does Aristotle say the route to virtue is, and what is it not?
cards.answer: Practice, not contemplation. You do not become virtuous by thinking about virtue — the habits are what create the identity, so character follows from what is repeatedly done.

cards.title: Eudaimonia
cards.prompt: Why are the best periods of a life the ones spent climbing rather than arrived?
cards.answer: Because the machinery rewards forward motion, not arrival. It is the same circuitry gambling exploits — pointed, here, at something that builds you.

cards.title: Executive Control Network
cards.prompt: What is the relationship between the executive control and default mode networks?
cards.answer: They alternate — when one is up the other quiets. Outward effortful focus and inward mind-wandering are two states of the same switch, not two things that run together.

cards.title: Executive Control Network
cards.prompt: What triggers the handoff from executive control to autopilot?
cards.answer: Prediction matching reality. When the world is doing what the brain expected — straight road, green lights, familiar route — conscious oversight is pulled offline to conserve fuel.

cards.title: Executive Control Network
cards.prompt: Why does the brain resist running the executive control network?
cards.answer: It burns glucose fast and exhausts quickly. The capacity is genuinely powerful but metabolically expensive, so the default is to shed it as soon as circumstances allow.

cards.title: Executive Function
cards.prompt: What does this page qualify without dismissing, in the discipline-based accounts?
cards.answer: Effort still matters — what varies is its price. The cost of producing the same behavioural evidence is not uniform across brains, so identical output is not identical exertion.

cards.title: Executive Function
cards.prompt: What does treating executive function as neurological first change about "laziness"?
cards.answer: It makes initiation failure architectural rather than moral. The same task genuinely costs different amounts across brains, so the behaviour is evidence about the system, not about the character.

cards.title: Executive Function
cards.prompt: What is invisible about a successful executive-function workaround?
cards.answer: Its cost. The workaround is built and paid for on top of the work itself, and observers see only the equivalent outcome — so the extra energy never enters anyone’s assessment.

cards.title: Fasting & Cognitive Performance
cards.prompt: What does feeling mentally clear during a fast fail to verify?
cards.answer: Ketosis, autophagy, immune repair or superior objective performance.

cards.title: Fasting & Cognitive Performance
cards.prompt: Why can the fasting source’s hour-by-hour timeline not be treated as universal?
cards.answer: It supplies no measurements, while diet, activity, health, medication and metabolism can shift the state.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: How does the thermostat enforce itself through spending?
cards.answer: By consuming money before it can be invested. Spending down to the familiar range keeps the balance inside the comfort zone without any conscious decision to stay poor.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Which part of the childhood money memory is the error, on this account?
cards.answer: Not the memory or the feeling — both were real. The error is the generalisation drawn from it: that money above a particular level means danger.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why can the financial ceiling not be argued away?
cards.answer: Because the amygdala updates on evidence, not reasoning. Exposure and survived actions are what change the threat tag; understanding the mechanism intellectually leaves the alarm exactly where it was.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why does "the whole thing is rigged" get read as a fear response rather than a position?
cards.answer: Because it makes inaction feel like a political stance. The conclusion happens to license exactly the behaviour the ceiling requires, which is what marks it as a rationalisation.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why does earning above the ceiling feel physically threatening?
cards.answer: Money is processed through the amygdala rather than the prefrontal cortex. Considering income above the setpoint fires the same alarm as physical danger, so the body treats the opportunity as a threat.

cards.title: Financial Thermostat
cards.prompt: Why does the diagnostic depend on the first number rather than a considered one?
cards.answer: Because the ceiling is subconscious. Anything after the first reflex has been through rationalisation or aspirational inflation, both of which edit the belief you were trying to read.

cards.title: Flow State
cards.prompt: How can a morning of scrolling prevent an afternoon of flow?
cards.answer: It spends the dopamine baseline. The mesocortical dopamine flow requires is no longer available, so the conditions cannot be assembled however good the environment is.

cards.title: Flow State
cards.prompt: Which phase of the flow cycle do most people quit in, and why is quitting there wrong?
cards.answer: Struggle. It is uncomfortable and feels like nothing is happening, but it is the initiation phase — the discomfort is the on-ramp rather than evidence the session has failed.

cards.title: Flow State
cards.prompt: Why does a task that is too easy block flow as reliably as one that is too hard?
cards.answer: Both leave the challenge-skill band. Too easy produces boredom, too hard produces anxiety; the state only appears in the narrow stretch just above current ability.

cards.title: Flow State
cards.prompt: Why does flow feel effortless when the work is demanding?
cards.answer: The prefrontal cortex partially deactivates, taking self-monitoring, self-criticism and time perception with it. The effort is still happening; what is missing is the running evaluation of it.

cards.title: Flow State
cards.prompt: Why is recovery mandatory rather than optional in the flow cycle?
cards.answer: Because pushing through it does not produce more flow. It depletes the system, so the cost is charged to the next session’s quality rather than paid now.

cards.title: Flow State
cards.prompt: Why write down open loops before a deep work session?
cards.answer: Unresolved items keep the default mode network surfacing them mid-session. Externalising them removes the reason for the interruption rather than requiring you to resist it.

cards.title: Free Will
cards.prompt: What agency does Libet's own veto proposal preserve?
cards.answer: Not initiation but interruption. If consciousness cannot start an action but can stop one, the experience of choosing may really be the experience of selectively not vetoing.

cards.title: Free Will
cards.prompt: What did Libet's readiness potential establish about the timing of a decision?
cards.answer: In Libet’s constrained motor task, a readiness potential preceded the subject’s reported intention time. It establishes pre-conscious preparation, not that every choice is fully determined before awareness.

cards.title: Free Will
cards.prompt: Where does agency relocate to, if moment-to-moment choice is automatic?
cards.answer: To the layer that generates the automatic choices — habits, beliefs and environments. The individual decision may be determined while the system producing it remains modifiable.

cards.title: Free Will
cards.prompt: Where does whatever freedom exists actually live, on the observer account?
cards.answer: In the gap between a thought arising and being identified with. The thought is generated either way; noticing it without becoming it is the whole of the available room.

cards.title: Free Will
cards.prompt: Why does limited free will argue for upstream intervention rather than for resignation?
cards.answer: Because the point of decision is where agency is weakest. Removing the temptation before that moment applies control where it still exists, instead of spending willpower where the outcome is already largely set.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: What does imaging show happening to the brain during dreaming?
cards.answer: Two opposite moves at once — the prefrontal region handling reasoning, reality-checking and suppression powers down, while the emotional core becomes more active than when awake.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: What is the difference between the questions Freud and Jung put to a dream?
cards.answer: Jung asked who you are beneath the mask; Freud asked what is hidden under it and why you put it there. One reads dreams as revelation of a self, the other as concealment of a wish.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: Which dreams are worth attending to, on Freud's account?
cards.answer: The ones that land hard — waking you with your heart going, or staying with you all day. Emotional charge is the signal that something was sent up rather than merely generated.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: Why are dreams incoherent, if their meaning is real?
cards.answer: The editor is offline. Morphing faces and impossible places are what raw emotion looks like without the machinery that normally makes experience coherent — the packaging is a mess, not the content.

cards.title: Freudian Dream Theory
cards.prompt: Why does a wish have to appear in a dream disguised?
cards.answer: Because the dream is a compromise. The unconscious wants something the conscious mind rejects, so the desire is admitted in a form that gets past what is left of the censor.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: What does the case of the lonely person with thousands of followers demonstrate?
cards.answer: That attention and connection are different goods. Every metric a lonely person imagines would help was maxed out, and none of it touched the thing that was missing.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: Why do established friend groups stay closed even to someone who fits?
cards.answer: The barrier is history, not compatibility. The shared language was invented while you were elsewhere, and it cannot be joined retroactively however well you would suit the group.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: Why does the friendship recession get read as structural rather than personal?
cards.answer: Because connections rose while real friendships fell — the two curves diverge across every age group. Environments optimised for reach rather than depth explain a population-level pattern that individual failings cannot.

cards.title: Friendship Recession
cards.prompt: Why is childhood friendship easy and adult friendship not?
cards.answer: Childhood supplies the whole formula for free — proximity plus hours. Adulthood requires schedules, values, emotional availability, trust and vulnerability to align at once, with nothing arranging that on your behalf.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: What is the characteristic waste of a signalling arms race?
cards.answer: Everyone spends more and nobody moves. The absolute cost of the signal rises while relative positions stay exactly where they were, because the signal only ever measured the gap.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: What makes the prisoner's dilemma a dilemma rather than a mistake?
cards.answer: Both players choose correctly given what the other might do, and both end up worse than if they had cooperated. The bad outcome is produced by rationality, not by error.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: Why does a bad standard like QWERTY survive?
cards.answer: Because the payoff comes from everyone doing the same thing, not from doing the best thing. A better standard loses to an entrenched one unless everybody switches at once.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: Why does repetition change the optimal strategy so completely?
cards.answer: Because future encounters give today’s behaviour a price. In a one-shot game defection has no consequence; repeated, it destroys the reputation that determines every subsequent round.

cards.title: Game Theory
cards.prompt: Why look at the incentive structure before judging the person inside it?
cards.answer: Because the same structure produces the same behaviour from most people in it. A broken incentive explains the conduct better than character does, and it is the part that can be changed.

cards.title: Glymphatic System
cards.prompt: What physically changes in the brain during deep sleep to allow clearance?
cards.answer: The interstitial space between brain cells expands by roughly 60%, letting cerebrospinal fluid flow far more freely through the tissue and carry waste out.

cards.title: Glymphatic System
cards.prompt: Why can't you make up glymphatic clearance by sleeping in?
cards.answer: The authors place the strongest clearance in slow-wave-rich early sleep. That supports protecting a regular full sleep opportunity; it does not show that recovery sleep is useless.

cards.title: Glymphatic System
cards.prompt: Why does the brain need a waste-clearance system of its own?
cards.answer: It is enclosed in the skull and walled off by the blood-brain barrier, so it cannot use the standard lymphatic network — while generating heavy waste on about 20% of the body’s energy budget.

cards.title: Glymphatic System
cards.prompt: Why is poor sleep treated as a possible cause of Alzheimer's rather than only a symptom?
cards.answer: The sources describe sleep-dependent clearance as one plausible link between sleep disruption and beta-amyloid burden. A short-term biomarker change does not by itself prove that each missed night adds permanent plaque.

cards.title: Goal Announcement Effect
cards.prompt: What distinguishes going quiet while building from hiding?
cards.answer: The motive. Hiding comes from fear of being seen; going quiet is a decision to keep the drive intact — the same silence sourced from the opposite place.

cards.title: Goal Announcement Effect
cards.prompt: Why does being congratulated on a goal reduce the chance of achieving it?
cards.answer: The acknowledgment registers as reward for progress already made. Having taken a bite of the prize, the drive that was going to fund the work deflates.

cards.title: Goal Announcement Effect
cards.prompt: Why is there no good response to an announced goal?
cards.answer: Both branches cost. A discouraging reply plants doubt you did not ask for; an encouraging one is a dopamine loan against work you have not done.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: How does a raise become part of the trap rather than an escape from it?
cards.answer: Expenses expand to fill it. After a few years the salary that felt like freedom is the minimum required to maintain the life built on it, so the increase bought no slack.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: Why is "I can't take risks, I have rent to pay" at 25 a self-fulfilling statement?
cards.answer: Acting on it builds the obligations that make it more true at 35 and more true again at 45. The sentence installs the conditions that justify it.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: Why is leaving a well-paid role costlier than losing the income?
cards.answer: Because the role became the identity. “I’m a senior manager at X” is the social self-concept and the basis of the professional relationships, so leaving forfeits those as well as the salary.

cards.title: Golden Handcuffs
cards.prompt: Why must the two escape moves happen simultaneously?
cards.answer: Because either alone leaves the trap intact. Cutting obligations without building income means no route out; building income while inflating lifestyle means the new income is consumed before it can fund anything.

cards.title: Grind Culture
cards.prompt: What changed about the comparison set that intensifies grind culture?
cards.answer: Its size and its editing. The reference group is now millions of people online, each showing only their highlights, so the standard being measured against is both enormous and fictional.

cards.title: Grind Culture
cards.prompt: What does constant work mode prevent, neurologically?
cards.answer: Consolidation. Learning is integrated during downtime and insight surfaces there too, so eliminating rest removes the phase where the work becomes usable.

cards.title: Grind Culture
cards.prompt: What is a publicly posted 4am wake-up actually optimising for?
cards.answer: The appearance of productivity. The metric being served is the visible signal of effort, which can be maximised without anything being built.

cards.title: Grind Culture
cards.prompt: What is the correction to grind culture, and what is it not?
cards.answer: Not the abandonment of goals — pure comfort is the other failure mode. It is building something meaningful while also living, which rejects the premise that the two compete.

cards.title: Grind Culture
cards.prompt: Why can "suffer now, enjoy later" never pay out?
cards.answer: Because the baseline moves with the achievement. Each milestone is adapted to and the next has to be larger, so the moment of arrival keeps receding.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: What is the horn effect?
cards.answer: The halo running in reverse. A negative first impression generates assumptions of other negative traits by the same automatic extension, with no evidence for them either.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: What makes the Jeremy Meeks case a strong demonstration of the halo effect?
cards.answer: The context was maximally unfavourable. A mugshot arrives labelled with a conviction, and the attractiveness still overrode it at scale — so the extension is not merely absence of contrary information.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: Which two signals does the halo effect run on?
cards.answer: Physical attractiveness, generating assumptions of competence, intelligence and moral character; and projected confidence, generating assumptions of expertise, authority and trustworthiness.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: Why does a bias this crude survive rather than being trained out?
cards.answer: Because it is economically efficient. Extending a judgement from one salient signal produces roughly serviceable predictions at almost no cost, where case-by-case evaluation is expensive.

cards.title: Halo Effect
cards.prompt: Why is the confidence halo systematically misallocated?
cards.answer: Because certainty is highest early on the expertise curve. The signal the brain reads as knowledge is most abundant in exactly the people who have least of it.

cards.title: Hard Problem of Consciousness
cards.prompt: What makes the hard problem hard rather than merely unsolved?
cards.answer: The easy problems are questions about mechanism, which more research answers in kind. The hard problem asks why any mechanism is accompanied by experience at all — a question no amount of mechanistic detail addresses.

cards.title: Hard Problem of Consciousness
cards.prompt: Why does epiphenomenalism threaten free will specifically?
cards.answer: If subjective experience is a byproduct that causes nothing, then the conscious deliberation you experience is not what produced the action. The feeling of choosing would be a report, not a cause.

cards.title: Hard Problem of Consciousness
cards.prompt: Why would a complete map of every neuron firing still leave the problem open?
cards.answer: Because it would describe what the brain does without explaining why doing it is accompanied by anything. Red could be processed perfectly by a system for which nothing looks like anything.

cards.title: Heartbreak as Growth
cards.prompt: What can heartbreak reveal that comfort cannot?
cards.answer: Actual limits rather than stated ones, real needs rather than assumed wants, and the patterns that repeat regardless of partner. Comfort insulates against exactly the questions that answer those.

cards.title: Heartbreak as Growth
cards.prompt: What is the grief phase doing, neurochemically?
cards.answer: Recalibrating the baseline after a sustained elevated state. The drop is the system returning from a level the relationship was maintaining, which is why it presents like withdrawal.

cards.title: Heartbreak as Growth
cards.prompt: Why does heartbreak produce genuine physical pain?
cards.answer: Social loss can recruit some of the same pain-related systems discussed in the source. That overlap does not reduce heartbreak to an “oxytocin loss” mechanism.

cards.title: Hedonic Treadmill
cards.prompt: How does social comparison accelerate the treadmill?
cards.answer: The treadmill adapts in absolute terms; comparison keeps raising the reference point. A curated feed of the most impressive examples worldwide guarantees the baseline creeps faster than any achievement can.

cards.title: Hedonic Treadmill
cards.prompt: What are the two horns of the self-improvement trap?
cards.answer: Achievement orientation, which defers satisfaction permanently because the promise moves each time it is met; and comfort seeking, which suppresses wanting without producing meaning.

cards.title: Hedonic Treadmill
cards.prompt: What makes the hedonic treadmill the same mechanism as drug tolerance?
cards.answer: Both can show diminishing response after repetition. The corpus uses dopamine tolerance as an analogy, but does not show that ordinary achievement and drug dependence are one mechanism differing only in substance.

cards.title: Hedonic Treadmill
cards.prompt: Why is a life organised around meaning less exposed to the treadmill than one organised around achievement?
cards.answer: Because meaning is located in the activity rather than the arrival. There is no destination to adapt to, so there is no reference point that resets after reaching it.

cards.title: Hedonic Treadmill
cards.prompt: Why is hedonic adaptation a design feature rather than a defect?
cards.answer: A system that stayed satisfied would stop seeking resources or status. Permanent satisfaction removes the motivation the reward system exists to supply.

cards.title: Heraclitean Flux
cards.prompt: What biological evidence is offered that the self is rebuilt daily?
cards.answer: Cells die overnight and are replaced, neurotransmitter levels differ morning to morning, and sleep consolidates the day by either myelinating a pathway or letting it fade. You wake as a slightly different machine.

cards.title: Heraclitean Flux
cards.prompt: What does "this is just who I am" get wrong, on the flux view?
cards.answer: It treats a process as an object. The self is being rebuilt continuously, so a fixed self-description is a description of one frame mistaken for the whole thing.

cards.title: Heraclitean Flux
cards.prompt: What does daily rebuilding imply about what you read, watch and who you sit near?
cards.answer: That they are construction material, not entertainment. Whatever is consolidated tonight builds the person who wakes tomorrow, so the inputs are the raw supply for the next version.

cards.title: Heraclitean Flux
cards.prompt: What is not optional in the flux argument, and what is?
cards.answer: The change is not optional — it happens daily regardless. What is optional is whether you steer it or let the inputs be chosen for you.

cards.title: Hormesis
cards.prompt: What are the two halves of a hormetic dose?
cards.answer: A threat large enough to wake the cell’s defences, and a recovery period afterwards. Without the second half it is not hormesis — it is just damage.

cards.title: Hormesis
cards.prompt: What separates the stress that strengthens from the stress that ages you?
cards.answer: Whether it ends. One is a sharp signal that terminates; the other hums in the background forever, and the humming is what does the damage.

cards.title: Hormesis
cards.prompt: Why should a fasting protocol be staged in rather than started cold turkey?
cards.answer: Because the limbic system will demand food for the first two or three weeks. Attempting the full protocol immediately fails for the same reason quitting smoking cold turkey does — the resistance peaks before any adaptation has happened.

cards.title: HPA Axis & Cortisol
cards.prompt: What does "tired but wired at 11pm" indicate about the cortisol curve?
cards.answer: That it has inverted. Cortisol is arriving in the evening instead of the morning, which is the late-phase burnout signature rather than a sleep-hygiene problem.

cards.title: HPA Axis & Cortisol
cards.prompt: What is burnout, mechanically, if not tiredness?
cards.answer: A disrupted cortisol rhythm. Early phase over-fires in the morning; late phase inverts entirely — flat on waking and wired at night, because the feedback loop has broken.

cards.title: HPA Axis & Cortisol
cards.prompt: Which brain structure physically shrinks under chronic cortisol, and what does it govern?
cards.answer: The hippocampus — memory and emotional regulation. The damage is structural, not a matter of feeling worse.

cards.title: HPA Axis & Cortisol
cards.prompt: Why does a 2pm coffee still affect sleep at midnight?
cards.answer: Caffeine’s half-life runs 8–12 hours. Enough remains in circulation at bedtime to keep cortisol elevated in the window where it should be at its lowest.

cards.title: HPA Axis & Cortisol
cards.prompt: Why is a large morning cortisol spike protective rather than harmful?
cards.answer: Because of the negative feedback loop. The morning peak suppresses further production for the rest of the day, so a strong ignition is what buys the evening quiet.

cards.title: HPA Axis & Cortisol
cards.prompt: Why is morning bright light the correct kind of cortisol boost?
cards.answer: It amplifies the natural peak rather than stacking artificial stress on top of it. Activating the suprachiasmatic nucleus raises cortisol roughly 50% at the moment the rhythm is already rising.

cards.title: Human Archetypes
cards.prompt: What three parts define an archetype in this framework?
cards.answer: A core insecurity, a desired identity, and the gap between the two. The gap is what anything sold or persuaded is actually addressing.

cards.title: Human Archetypes
cards.prompt: Why can a 20ebookanda2,000 course serve the same buyer equally?
cards.answer: Because what is being bought is the bridge across the gap, not the artefact. Price tracks how the gap is framed, not the content delivered.

cards.title: Human Archetypes
cards.prompt: Why does the archetype predict behaviour better than someone's stated reasons?
cards.answer: Because the pattern runs below conscious awareness. The stated reasons are generated after the fact by someone with no access to the thing actually driving the behaviour.

cards.title: Human Archetypes
cards.prompt: Why does the aspiring entrepreneur keep buying courses?
cards.answer: Because buying feels like progress. The purchase delivers the sensation of moving without the exposure of starting, which is precisely the pain it was meant to resolve.

cards.title: Human Archetypes
cards.prompt: Why translate "evidence-based hypertrophy protocol" into "a physique that makes people respect you"?
cards.answer: The first describes the product; the second names the desired identity. Persuasion runs through the gap the person actually feels, not through the accurate description of the mechanism.

cards.title: Icarus Myth (Reframed)
cards.prompt: What does never attempting the thing preserve?
cards.answer: The fantasy. Trying and failing settles the question about your capacity; never trying leaves the possibility of greatness intact precisely because it is never tested.

cards.title: Icarus Myth (Reframed)
cards.prompt: What is the actual choice, if not between safety and risk?
cards.answer: Between risks you choose — ambition, failure, exposure — and risks chosen for you — stagnation, atrophy, regret. Both carry costs; the question is whose terms they are on.

cards.title: Icarus Myth (Reframed)
cards.prompt: Which fact does the conventional Icarus reading leave out?
cards.answer: That they were prisoners. Once the labyrinth is a prison, the “safe” option is captivity and the flight is an escape rather than an overreach.

cards.title: Icarus Myth (Reframed)
cards.prompt: Why is "don't fly too high" treated as non-neutral advice?
cards.answer: Because it serves the interests of whoever benefits from you staying in your assigned place. The counsel arrives from inside a structure that gains from your compliance with it.

cards.title: Id, Ego and Superego
cards.prompt: If the internal conflict is permanent, what is the achievable goal?
cards.answer: Awareness of it. Victory is impossible — the three keep arguing for life. What is available is ceasing to be an unwitting casualty of a war you did not know was running.

cards.title: Id, Ego and Superego
cards.prompt: What is Freud's darker claim about the child's tantrum?
cards.answer: That it does not disappear, it gets buried. The same force resurfaces in adult form as the unaffordable purchase and the explosion over something small.

cards.title: Id, Ego and Superego
cards.prompt: What is the ego's function in the three-way conflict?
cards.answer: Negotiation, not judgment. It finds the move that partly satisfies the impulse without incurring the punishment — update the resume rather than either quitting on the spot or doing nothing.

cards.title: Id, Ego and Superego
cards.prompt: What principle does the id run on, and what is it indifferent to?
cards.answer: The pleasure principle — immediate satisfaction. It is indifferent to consequence, morality and social judgment, which is why it produces the 2am text you already know the ending of.

cards.title: Id, Ego and Superego
cards.prompt: Why does a superego rule keep operating after you consciously reject it?
cards.answer: Because it was installed before the capacity to evaluate it. The disapproving look got encoded as an internal standard, so the shame fires whether or not you still endorse the rule producing it.

cards.title: Identity Setpoint
cards.prompt: Why does sabotage cluster just before a breakthrough rather than at the start?
cards.answer: Because proximity is the trigger. As the goal nears, the system detects that the identity model is about to be violated, and corrects before the violation lands.

cards.title: Identity Setpoint
cards.prompt: Why does the identity setpoint correct upward deviations as well as downward ones?
cards.answer: Because what it enforces is consistency, not quality. A windfall, a promotion or a reached fitness goal all violate the model, and the system restores baseline in whichever direction the deviation ran.

cards.title: Identity Setpoint
cards.prompt: Why does the nervous system treat leaving a bad situation as the threat?
cards.answer: Because it optimises for predictability rather than wellbeing. The toxicity is modelled and its consequences known; the exit is not — so the unfamiliar better option scores as the more dangerous one.

cards.title: Identity Shift
cards.prompt: What is the failure sequence when identity is claimed before evidence exists?
cards.answer: Social recognition pays out early, motivation to produce the evidence drops, no evidence follows, and the identity claim collapses — leaving the person further from the change than before they announced it.

cards.title: Identity Shift
cards.prompt: Why do affirmations alone fail to shift identity?
cards.answer: The self-model updates on evidence, not on statements. An action consistent with the new identity is a data point the brain can count; a claim about yourself is not.

cards.title: Identity Shift
cards.prompt: Why does behaviour-first change require permanent willpower while identity-first does not?
cards.answer: Behaviour contradicting the self-model generates resistance that has to be overcome every time. Once the model itself updates, the same behaviour is what the model predicts, so nothing is being fought.

cards.title: Ikigai
cards.prompt: What does clear purpose predict, beyond life satisfaction?
cards.answer: The source reports associations with lower distress, immune function, and longevity. Those associations do not establish that purpose alone causes the physiological outcomes.

cards.title: Ikigai
cards.prompt: What is the correction to "finding your ikigai"?
cards.answer: That it is constructed rather than discovered. It is built iteration by iteration, so waiting to locate it fully formed is waiting for something that does not arrive that way.

cards.title: Ikigai
cards.prompt: Which four questions have to intersect for ikigai?
cards.answer: What you love, what you are good at, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for. Any three without the fourth is something else.

cards.title: Ikigai
cards.prompt: Why start with love and skill rather than trying to solve all four at once?
cards.answer: Because the other two are downstream of depth. What the world needs and what it will pay for only become visible once you are far enough into something to see where it is useful.

cards.title: Maladaptive Daydreaming
cards.prompt: What makes immersive daydreaming maladaptive in the source's account?
cards.answer: Functional displacement. Vividness alone is not the threshold; the pattern becomes maladaptive when fantasy repeatedly replaces presence, relationships, work, or action.

cards.title: Insecurity
cards.prompt: Why does avoidance preserve insecurity even when it prevents immediate embarrassment?
cards.answer: Because the absence of rejection is credited to concealment. The original danger rule is never tested, so no evidence accumulates that authentic expression can be safe.

cards.title: Interest-Based Attention
cards.prompt: What distinguishes an interest-based attention system from a voluntary one?
